features.title: Abkhazia and South Ossetia: part of Georgia, or shown as states
features.subject: Abkhazia and South Ossetia

states.label: No borders of their own
states.question: Are Abkhazia and South Ossetia drawn as part of the country around them, with no borders of their own?
states.claim: Abkhazia and S. Ossetia are unmarked
states.cue: Inside the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union and then Georgia. Some maps print their names or dash their edges since the wars of the early 1990s, but with Georgia's colour.

states.label: Recognised by Russia
states.question: Are Abkhazia and South Ossetia shown as countries of their own?
states.cue: Since August 2008 Russia recognises both as states; Russian maps give them their own colours and borders. Other maps keep them in Georgia.

depictions.label: Shown as countries
depictions.question: Are Abkhazia and South Ossetia shown as countries of their own, with their own colour and borders?
depictions.claim: Abkhazia and S. Ossetia are countries
depictions.cue: Russian maps since 2009 colour Abkhazia and South Ossetia apart from Georgia, with full country borders.

depictions.label: Still part of Georgia
depictions.question: Are Abkhazia and South Ossetia drawn as part of Georgia, with no borders of their own?
depictions.cue: Almost all maps outside Russia keep both inside Georgia, sometimes dashed or labelled as breakaway regions.

transitions.funFact: Two weeks after its five-day war with Georgia in August 2008, Russia recognised Abkhazia and South Ossetia as countries. Hardly anyone followed: Nicaragua, Venezuela, Syria and tiny Nauru did, while Tuvalu and Vanuatu signed up and later backed out, as Nauru itself did in July 2026.

features.title: Nigeria's capital: Lagos or Abuja
features.subject: Nigeria

states.label: Lagos
states.question: Is Lagos, on the coast, Nigeria's capital?
states.cue: The capital star at Lagos on the coast; inland there is no Abuja, or only a small town.

states.label: Abuja
states.question: Is Abuja, in the middle of the country, Nigeria's capital?
states.cue: The capital star at Abuja in the centre of Nigeria; Lagos is shown as an ordinary (big) city.

transitions.funFact: Nigeria chose a new capital in 1976 for the same reason as Brazil had: a neutral site in the middle, away from the three big ethnic regions and the chaos of overcrowded Lagos. Abuja was built from scratch through the 1980s, and the government moved in on 12 December 1991.

features.title: Acre: Bolivian or Brazilian
features.subject: Western Amazon

states.label: Bolivian
states.question: Does Bolivia reach north into the Amazon, taking in the Acre region?
states.cue: Bolivia's colour runs far north up the Purus and Acre rivers, so the rubber land of Acre is Bolivian and Brazil ends further east.

states.label: Brazilian
states.question: Is Acre part of Brazil, with Bolivia's northern border pulled back south?
states.cue: Brazil's colour covers Acre in the far west, and Bolivia's northern border follows the Abunã and Acre rivers; Acre is often labelled as a Brazilian territory.

transitions.funFact: Acre was Bolivian on paper but full of Brazilian rubber tappers, who rebelled several times; in 1899 a Spanish adventurer, Luis Gálvez, even proclaimed a Republic of Acre. In the Treaty of Petrópolis Brazil bought the region for £2 million, a strip of land elsewhere and a promise to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway around the river's rapids.

features.title: Albania: Ottoman, independent, or united with Italy
features.subject: Albania

states.label: Part of the Ottoman Empire
states.question: Is Albania part of Turkey (the Ottoman Empire)?
states.cue: No Albania: the Ottoman (Turkish) colour runs along the Adriatic from Montenegro to Greece.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Albania an independent country in its own colour?
states.cue: Albania has its own colour, with the capital at Tirana (Durrës on maps before 1920).

states.label: United with Italy
states.question: Is Albania in Italy's colour, united with the Italian crown?
states.cue: Albania shares Italy's colour or is labelled Albania (It.), "Italian Albania" or Albania (Ital.). Only on maps of 1939 to about 1943.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Albania an independent country in its own colour?
states.cue: Albania has its own colour, with the capital at Tirana.

transitions.funFact: Albania declared independence from the Ottoman Empire at Vlorë in November 1912, during the First Balkan War. The great powers recognised it in 1913 and drew its borders, leaving many Albanians outside them.

Italy invaded on Good Friday, 7 April 1939, and King Zog fled to Greece with part of the national bank's gold. Days later Albania's crown passed to the King of Italy. Hergé later said this crisis inspired the Syldavia of his Tintin story King Ottokar's Sceptre.

When Italy dropped out of the war in September 1943, the union collapsed. German troops occupied the country and restored a nominally independent Albania, until Enver Hoxha's Communist partisans took power in late 1944 and ruled for four decades.

features.title: Algeria: the coastal north only, or deep into the Sahara
features.subject: Algeria

states.label: Coast and north only
states.question: Does Algeria stop at the edge of the Sahara?
states.claim: Algeria stops at the desert's edge
states.cue: Algeria's colour covers the coast, the Atlas and the northern oases; the Sahara further south is blank, "Sahara", or part of French West Africa.

states.label: Deep into the Sahara
states.question: Does Algeria reach deep into the Sahara?
states.claim: Algeria reaches deep into the Sahara
states.cue: Algeria's colour runs some 2,000 km south from the coast, through the desert to the edge of the Sahel.

transitions.funFact: Algeria owes its huge size to a French law of December 1902 that attached the newly conquered Saharan oases to it as the "Southern Territories", run by the army. At independence in 1962 Algeria kept the whole desert, and today it is Africa's largest country.

features.title: Name of Kazakhstan's biggest city
features.subject: City below the Tian Shan, Kazakhstan

states.label: Verny
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Verny ('faithful'), a Russian fort founded in 1854.

states.label: Alma-Ata
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Alma-Ata, 1921-1993; capital of Soviet Kazakhstan from 1929.

states.label: Almaty
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Almaty, the Kazakh form, since 1993; Russian maps keep Алма-Ата.

transitions.funFact: The Soviets replaced the tsarist fort name Verny, Russian for 'faithful', with Alma-Ata in February 1921. The name was taken to mean 'father of apples': the wild apple forests on the slopes above the city are thought to be where the ancestor of the cultivated apple first grew.

After independence Kazakhstan adopted the Kazakh form Almaty, roughly 'place of apples'. It was the capital until December 1997, when President Nazarbayev moved the government 1,000 km north to the steppe city that became Astana; Almaty is still the country's biggest city.

features.title: Sudan: Mahdist state, Anglo-Egyptian Sudan or independent Sudan
features.subject: Upper Nile

states.label: Mahdist state
states.question: Is the Sudan left without the Anglo-Egyptian label, as the Mahdi's state or a lost Egyptian Sudan?
states.cue: No Anglo-Egyptian Sudan: the land south of Egypt is uncoloured or labelled Egyptian Sudan, Soudan, Mahdist State or Dervishes, usually with no borders to the south and west.

ja: エジプト領スーダン (マフディー国家)

states.label: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
states.question: Is Sudan shown as the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, ruled jointly by Britain and Egypt?
states.cue: Labelled Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (Ang.-Eg. Sudan, Soudan anglo-égyptien), usually in Britain's colour or striped with Egypt's.

ja: イギリス・エジプト領スーダン

states.label: Independent Sudan
states.question: Is Sudan an independent country with its own colour?
states.cue: Just "Sudan", in its own colour. Until 2011 it was Africa's largest country, including what is now South Sudan.

transitions.funFact: In 1885 the Mahdi's army stormed Khartoum and killed General Gordon, and for thirteen years Sudan was a Mahdist state ruled from Omdurman. Kitchener's army destroyed it at Omdurman in September 1898 with machine guns and artillery, losing fewer than fifty men against some 11,000 Mahdist dead. The agreement of January 1899 made Sudan a joint Anglo-Egyptian possession.

Britain and Egypt had ruled Sudan jointly since 1899, though Britain held the real power. After Egypt's 1952 revolution both sides agreed to let the Sudanese choose, and the country became independent on 1 January 1956, as the largest country in Africa.

features.title: Angora or Ankara
features.subject: Turkey's capital

states.label: Angora
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Angora, the old Western name, as in Angora cats, goats and wool.

states.label: Ankara
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Ankara (Ancara), the Turkish name used on maps after 1930.

transitions.funFact: Angora gave its name to the fluffy Angora rabbit, goat and cat long before it replaced Constantinople as Turkey's capital in October 1923. From 1930 the city was officially Ankara in Western languages too, and by the late 1930s English maps had mostly dropped Angora.

features.title: Territorial claims in Antarctica: none, a few British wedges, most of the continent, or overlapping
features.subject: Antarctica

states.label: No claims
states.question: Is Antarctica drawn with no claim lines at all?
states.cue: One blank continent; at most the names of coasts after their explorers.

states.label: A few British and NZ wedges
states.question: Are there only a few claim wedges, with most of Antarctica unclaimed?
states.claim: Antarctica has a few claim wedges
states.cue: A British wedge south of the Falklands (Falkland Islands Dependencies), the Ross Dependency (N.Z.) south of New Zealand, perhaps a thin French Adélie Land; the rest is blank.

states.label: Australia claims a huge sector
states.question: Does a huge Australian sector cover most of East Antarctica?
states.claim: Australia claims most of East Antarctica
states.cue: The Australian Antarctic Territory covers about 42% of the continent, from below Madagascar's longitude almost to New Zealand's, split by the narrow French Adélie Land.

ja: オーストラリア南極領土

states.label: Claims almost all round
states.question: Do claims run almost all the way round, with Norway's Queen Maud Land filling the Atlantic side?
states.claim: Claims run almost all round Antarctica
states.cue: Queen Maud Land (Norway) fills the gap south of Africa; only the Pacific sector between the Ross Dependency and the British wedge (Marie Byrd Land) is unclaimed.

ja: クイーン・モード・ランド

states.label: Overlapping claims on the Peninsula
states.question: Do Chilean (and Argentine) wedges overlap the British one on the Antarctic Peninsula?
states.cue: South of South America the British, Chilean and later Argentine wedges overlap, often drawn with crossing lines or hatching.

depictions.label: Overlapping wedges
depictions.question: Do Chilean (and Argentine) wedges overlap the British one on the Antarctic Peninsula?
depictions.cue: Two or three wedges overlap south of South America.

depictions.label: Only the earlier wedges
depictions.question: Do claims run almost all the way round, with Norway's Queen Maud Land filling the Atlantic side?
depictions.claim: Claims run almost all round Antarctica
depictions.cue: Many maps never drew the Chilean and Argentine claims, or only the British one.

transitions.funFact: Britain was first, in 1908, claiming the islands and peninsula south of the Falklands, and in 1917 it stretched the claim into a wedge reaching the South Pole. In 1923 it added the Ross Dependency for New Zealand, so the first pie slices on globes were British.

In 1933 Britain handed Australia the largest claim of all: the Australian Antarctic Territory, about 5.9 million km² or 42 percent of Antarctica, roughly three quarters the size of Australia itself. Only the narrow French slice of Adélie Land interrupts it.

Norway claimed Queen Maud Land by royal decree on 14 January 1939, filling the gap south of Africa between the British and Australian sectors. That left a single slice, Marie Byrd Land in the Pacific, which nobody has ever claimed.

Chile claimed its own wedge in November 1940 and Argentina followed in the 1940s, both overlapping the British sector on the Antarctic Peninsula. The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze all claims without settling them, so the overlap is still drawn today.

features.title: Aouzou Strip: Chad's northern border, held by Libya
features.subject: Chad and Libya

states.label: No strip
states.question: Does the Chad–Libya border run across the desert with no strip marked along it?
states.claim: No strip is marked along Chad's border
states.cue: One straight-sided border from Niger to Sudan, with nothing hatched or dashed south of it.

states.label: Strip held by Libya
states.question: Is a strip of northern Chad hatched or marked as held by Libya?
states.claim: Northern Chad has a Libyan-held strip
states.cue: A band along the border, hatched or between two lines, labelled Aouzou Strip, "occupied by Libya" or "claimed by Libya".

depictions.label: Marked as disputed
depictions.question: Is a strip of northern Chad hatched or marked as held by Libya?
depictions.claim: Northern Chad has a Libyan-held strip
depictions.cue: A band along the border, hatched or between two lines, labelled Aouzou Strip, "occupied by Libya" or "claimed by Libya".

depictions.label: Part of Libya
depictions.question: Is the strip along Chad's northern border drawn as part of Libya?
depictions.claim: The Aouzou strip is part of Libya
depictions.cue: Libya's colour reaches about 100 km into what other maps call Chad, with the border along the strip's southern edge.

depictions.label: Not shown
depictions.question: Does the Chad–Libya border run across the desert with no strip marked along it?
depictions.claim: No strip is marked along Chad's border
depictions.cue: Drawn as if nothing had changed: the border from Niger to Sudan with no strip.

states.label: No strip
states.question: Does the Chad–Libya border run across the desert with no strip marked along it?
states.claim: No strip is marked along Chad's border
states.cue: One straight-sided border from Niger to Sudan, with nothing hatched or dashed south of it.

transitions.funFact: In 1935 Mussolini and France agreed to move this strip from French Chad to Italian Libya, but the treaty was never ratified. Gaddafi used it to justify occupying the mineral-rich strip in 1973. The war that followed ended with Chad's 1987 "Toyota War", fought largely from pickup trucks.

Chad and Libya let the World Court decide, and in February 1994 its judges ruled 16 to 1 for Chad. Libya actually left: the UN sent one of its smallest missions ever, fifteen people, to watch the withdrawal, which was finished within weeks.

features.title: The neutral zones on Saudi Arabia's borders with Iraq and Kuwait
features.subject: Northern edge of Saudi Arabia

states.label: No neutral zones
states.question: Are there no neutral zones on the borders south of Iraq and Kuwait?
states.claim: Arabia's northern borders are plain lines
states.cue: Plain borders: no diamond west of Kuwait and no "Neutral Zone" label on the coast.

states.label: Two neutral zones
states.question: Are there two neutral zones, a diamond on the Iraqi border and a block south of Kuwait?
states.cue: Two areas labelled Neutral Zone, usually hatched: a diamond between Iraq and Saudi Arabia and a rectangle on the coast south of Kuwait.

states.label: Only the diamond
states.question: Is there only one neutral zone, the diamond between Iraq and Saudi Arabia?
states.claim: There is one neutral zone, the diamond
states.cue: The diamond west of Kuwait is still labelled Neutral Zone, but the area south of Kuwait is split by a line between Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

states.label: No neutral zones
states.question: Are there no neutral zones on the borders south of Iraq and Kuwait?
states.claim: Arabia's northern borders are plain lines
states.cue: Plain borders: no diamond west of Kuwait and no "Neutral Zone" label on the coast.

transitions.funFact: At Uqair in 1922 the British envoy Sir Percy Cox drew the borders of Iraq, Kuwait and Ibn Saud's Nejd himself, in pencil on a map. Where the desert wells were shared by wandering Bedouin he left two neutral zones, owned by both sides at once.

Oil turned the Kuwaiti neutral zone from empty desert into a prize: wells drilled from 1953 pumped for both countries. In the late 1960s Kuwait and Saudi Arabia split the land down the middle, but kept sharing the oil beneath it.

Iraq and Saudi Arabia quietly divided their diamond in 1981 but never published the treaty, so for ten years the world's maps kept drawing a neutral zone that no longer existed. Only after Iraq invaded Kuwait did Saudi Arabia register the border with the UN, in June 1991.

features.title: Outline of the Aral Sea
features.subject: Aral Sea

states.label: One large lake
states.question: Is the Aral Sea one big lake?
states.claim: The Aral Sea is one big lake
states.cue: Look east of the Caspian Sea. Until the 1980s the Aral Sea is one large, roughly oval lake, about the size of Ireland, often dotted with small islands.

states.label: Two lakes
states.question: Has the Aral Sea split into two lakes?
states.claim: The Aral Sea is split into two lakes
states.cue: A small lake in the north and a larger, ragged one in the south. Some maps add a dotted line where the old shore used to be.

states.label: Mostly dry
states.question: Is the Aral Sea mostly dry?
states.claim: The Aral Sea is mostly dry
states.cue: Only a small northern lake and a thin strip in the west are left. The rest is drawn as desert or salt flats, often stippled where the water was.

transitions.funFact: From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton fields. With far less water flowing in, the lake shrank year after year, and around 1987-88 it split into a northern and a southern lake. Many maps kept drawing the old shoreline for years afterwards.

In August 2014 satellite images showed the eastern basin of the southern lake completely dry, probably for the first time in about 600 years. It had nearly dried out in 2009 too. Meanwhile a Kazakh dam finished in 2005 has helped the small northern lake to recover.

sources.title: The Aral Sea Loses Its Eastern Lobe (NASA Earth Observatory)

features.title: Name of the city on the Ishim, Kazakhstan
features.subject: City on the Ishim, Kazakhstan

states.label: Akmolinsk
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Akmolinsk, a steppe fort and market town founded in 1830.

states.label: Tselinograd
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Tselinograd, 'Virgin Lands City', 1961-1992.

states.label: Akmola
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Akmola, the Kazakh name restored after independence; capital from December 1997.

states.label: Astana
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Astana, 'the capital' in Kazakh, from 1998 to 2019 and again since 2022.

states.label: Nur-Sultan
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Nur-Sultan, after the first president, from March 2019 to September 2022.

states.label: Astana
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Astana again since September 2022.

transitions.funFact: In 1954 Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign sent hundreds of thousands of young volunteers to plough up the steppe of northern Kazakhstan, and Akmolinsk became its headquarters. On 20 March 1961 the town was renamed Tselinograd, Russian for 'Virgin Lands City'.

After Kazakhstan's independence the Soviet name was dropped and the city went back to a Kazakh form, Akmola. It is often translated as 'white grave' or 'white shrine', though historians argue about the origin. In December 1997 President Nazarbayev moved the capital there from Almaty.

A capital called 'White Grave' did not sound right, so in May 1998 Akmola was renamed Astana, which simply means 'capital' in Kazakh. A futuristic skyline grew up around the Bayterek tower and a giant see-through tent of a shopping centre designed by Norman Foster.

Three days after Nursultan Nazarbayev stepped down as president in March 2019, after almost 30 years in power, parliament renamed the capital Nur-Sultan in his honour. Some people who protested against the change were detained.

In September 2022, after deadly unrest that January had weakened Nazarbayev's hold on politics, President Tokayev signed a law giving the capital back the name Astana. Renamed five times since 1961, it holds a Guinness record for the capital with the most name changes in modern times.

features.title: Location of Australia's capital: Melbourne or Canberra
features.subject: Australia's capital

states.label: Melbourne (no Canberra)
states.question: Is there no capital star at Canberra, with Melbourne as the seat of government?
states.claim: Melbourne is the seat of government
states.cue: Melbourne carries the capital mark, or there is no national capital at all; Canberra is missing or only a site in a small 'Federal Territory'.

states.label: Canberra
states.question: Is the capital star at Canberra, inland between Sydney and Melbourne?
states.cue: The star sits at Canberra, in the Federal Capital Territory; Sydney and Melbourne are state capitals.

transitions.funFact: Sydney and Melbourne both wanted to be capital, so the constitution said it must be in New South Wales but at least 100 miles from Sydney, with Parliament sitting in Melbourne meanwhile. Canberra, named in 1913, comes from an old local place name, Canberry. Parliament moved in on 9 May 1927, into a 'provisional' house that served for 61 years.

features.title: Australia: six separate British colonies or the Commonwealth of Australia
features.subject: Australia

states.label: Six separate colonies
states.question: Are New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and the others separate colonies, with no Commonwealth of Australia?
states.cue: Each colony carries its own name and often its own tint: New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia (which then reached the north coast), Western Australia and Tasmania. Only the continent is called Australia.

ja: ニューサウスウェールズ

states.label: Commonwealth of Australia
states.question: Is Australia one country, the Commonwealth of Australia?
states.cue: One country label across the continent, Commonwealth of Australia or Australian Commonwealth; the former colonies remain as states, divided by thinner lines.

transitions.funFact: Six rival colonies, with their own defence forces, stamps, tariffs and even different railway gauges, became one country on 1 January 1901, proclaimed in Centennial Park, Sydney. Western Australia only voted to join on 31 July 1900, after London had already passed the act. New Zealand sat in on the early conventions but stayed out.

lookalikes.note: The colony names and borders live on as state names and borders after 1901

features.title: The Bahamas: British colony or independent country
features.subject: Islands east of Florida

states.label: British colony
states.question: Are the Bahamas a British colony, marked (Br.)?
states.cue: Britain's colour, or "(Br.)" or "(U.K.)" after the name.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Are the Bahamas an independent country, with no British mark?
states.cue: Their own colour and a plain name, with Nassau as a capital.

transitions.funFact: After three centuries as a British colony the Bahamas became independent on 10 July 1973, keeping the British monarch as head of state. The country is some 700 islands and over two thousand cays, but nearly three in four Bahamians live on one island, New Providence.

features.title: Status of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania
features.subject: Baltic states

states.label: Part of the Russian Empire
states.question: Are Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania part of Russia?
states.claim: The Baltic states are part of Russia
states.cue: There are no Baltic countries: Russia's colour runs right up to East Prussia. You may see old province names in small type, like Livland, Kurland or Estland.

states.label: Three independent countries
states.question: Are Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania independent countries?
states.cue: Three separate countries on the Baltic coast, each in its own colour with a capital star: Tallinn, Riga and Kaunas or Vilnius.

states.label: Part of the Soviet Union
states.question: Are the Baltic states part of the Soviet Union?
states.cue: The Soviet colour covers the coast all the way to Poland.

depictions.label: Plain part of the Soviet Union
depictions.question: Are the Baltic states plainly part of the Soviet Union?
depictions.claim: The Baltic states are plainly Soviet
depictions.cue: The Soviet colour covers the whole coast up to Poland. Names like Estonian SSR may appear, but nothing sets the three apart from the rest of the USSR.

depictions.label: Soviet, but marked as annexed
depictions.question: Are the Baltic states Soviet, but marked as annexed?
depictions.claim: The Baltic states are marked as annexed
depictions.cue: They're inside the Soviet Union but drawn apart: hatching, their own outline or colour, or a note that the annexation isn't recognised. Common on American and British maps from 1940 to 1991.

states.label: Three independent countries
states.question: Are Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania independent countries?
states.cue: Three separate countries on the Baltic coast, each in its own colour with a capital star: Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius.

transitions.funFact: As the Russian and German empires collapsed at the end of the First World War, Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia each declared independence during 1918. After wars of independence against Soviet Russia and others, Moscow recognised all three in peace treaties signed in 1920.

Under a secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Red Army occupied the three countries in June 1940, and in early August they were annexed as Soviet republics. The United States and most Western governments never recognised this, so many Western maps kept marking the region as occupied.

After the failed coup in Moscow in August 1991, Estonia and Latvia declared full independence, joining Lithuania, which had done so in March 1990. The Soviet Union recognised all three on 6 September 1991, less than four months before it ceased to exist itself.

features.title: Baikal–Amur Mainline: the second railway across Siberia
features.subject: Railways of eastern Siberia

states.label: No second railway
states.question: Is there no railway between the north tip of Lake Baikal and the Amur?
states.claim: No railway runs north of Baikal
states.cue: Only the Trans-Siberian, south of Baikal and along the Chinese border; at most short branches end at Ust-Kut on the Lena and at Komsomolsk.

states.label: Under construction
states.question: Is a second railway north of Baikal drawn dashed, as under construction?
states.claim: A railway north of Baikal is being built
states.cue: A dashed line, often labelled BAM or "under construction", from Ust-Kut past Baikal's north tip through Tynda to Komsomolsk.

states.label: Finished line
states.question: Does a second railway run all the way from Baikal's north tip to the Amur?
states.claim: A second railway runs north of Baikal
states.cue: A solid railway from Tayshet past the north end of Lake Baikal, through Tynda, to Komsomolsk-on-Amur and the Pacific at Sovetskaya Gavan.

transitions.funFact: Stalin's labour camps had started the BAM in the 1930s, but most of it was only begun in 1974, when Brezhnev called it "the construction project of the century". Young Komsomol volunteers flocked to lay 3,000 km of track through some of Siberia's harshest terrain.

The two halves of the BAM met in September 1984, celebrated with a "golden link" of track at Kuanda. But the line was barely usable: it took until 1989 to open fully, and the 15 km Severomuysky tunnel was finished only in 2003.

features.title: Spelling of China's northern capital
features.subject: China's capital

states.label: Peking (imperial / early republic)
states.question: Is the capital spelled {name}?
states.cue: Look in northern China, near the coast. Older maps print Peking (Pékin, Pechino) with a capital star.

states.label: Peiping
states.question: Is the capital spelled {name}?
states.cue: From 1928 to 1949 the government sat in Nanking, and the old capital was renamed Peiping, 'northern peace'. It loses its capital star.

states.label: Peking (People's Republic, before Pinyin)
states.question: Is the capital spelled {name}?
states.cue: The capital star is back, still with the old spelling. Most Western maps kept Peking until about 1979.

states.label: Beijing (Pinyin era)
states.question: Is the capital spelled {name}?
states.cue: The pinyin spelling, used on most maps from the early 1980s.

transitions.funFact: In 1928 the Nationalist government made Nanjing ('southern capital') the capital of China and renamed Beijing ('northern capital') to Beiping, 'northern peace', usually spelled Peiping on Western maps. Under Japanese occupation from 1937 to 1945 the old name came back, so wartime maps are inconsistent.

On 27 September 1949, days before Mao proclaimed the People's Republic, the new government restored the name Beijing and made the city the capital again. Western maps went back to the long-established spelling Peking, which came from older European romanisations.

From 1 January 1979 China asked foreign governments and media to use Pinyin spellings, so Peking became Beijing, Canton became Guangzhou and Tientsin became Tianjin. English-language atlases mostly switched within a few years, while Dutch, German, French and many other languages kept their traditional names.

features.title: Belize: British colony or independent country
features.subject: Caribbean coast of Central America

states.label: British colony
states.question: Is Belize (British Honduras) a British colony?
states.cue: British colour, or "(Br.)" or "(U.K.)" after the name; before 1973 the name itself is British Honduras.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Belize an independent country, with no British mark?
states.cue: Its own colour and plain name, Belize (Belice), with Belmopan as its capital.

transitions.funFact: Belize waited years for independence because Guatemala claimed the whole country as its own. When it finally came in September 1981, British troops stayed on to guard the border, and Guatemala recognised its neighbour only in 1991, ten years later.

features.title: British Honduras or Belize
features.subject: East of Guatemala

states.label: British Honduras
states.question: Is the territory called {name}?
states.cue: British Honduras (Br. Honduras, Honduras britannique).

ja: イギリス領ホンジュラス

On 5 February 1991, months before the Soviet Union fell, the city took the Kyrgyz name Bishkek. Legend links it to a hero called Bishkek Batyr; others point to the bishkek, a wooden paddle used to churn kumis, fermented mare's milk.

transitions.funFact: Bechuanaland was so poor and neglected that Britain governed it from Mafeking, a town outside its own borders, in South Africa. A new capital, Gaborone, was built almost from scratch for independence on 30 September 1966. A year later diamonds were found, and Botswana became one of Africa's richest countries.

transitions.funFact: When Czechoslovakia took the Hungarian coronation city of Pozsony in 1919, it needed a Slovak name. Slovak Americans suggested Wilsonov, after President Wilson, but the new state chose Bratislava, a form that grew out of a 19th-century scholar's misreading of a medieval name. It became official in March 1919.

transitions.funFact: Brasília was built almost from scratch on the empty central plateau in about four years and inaugurated on 21 April 1960, taking over from Rio de Janeiro. Moving the capital inland had been planned since Brazil's first republican constitution of 1891. Seen from above, Lúcio Costa's city plan looks like an aeroplane.

transitions.funFact: Brazil was the only lasting monarchy in the Americas until army officers deposed Emperor Pedro II on 15 November 1889, a year after his daughter Isabel signed the law ending slavery. The new regime copied its northern neighbour: its very first decree turned the provinces into states and the country into the United States of Brazil. The imperial family was sent into exile in Europe.

For 78 years Brazil's official name echoed the United States: Estados Unidos do Brasil. The military government's constitution of 1967 simply said Brazil, and a 1969 amendment added the name it still has, Federative Republic of Brazil. Most maps had long printed just Brazil, so on them nothing changed at all.

transitions.funFact: A sleepy river town became a city of half a million in the 1970s, when the Soviet Union built the world's biggest truck factory, KamAZ, there. Days after Leonid Brezhnev died in November 1982, it was renamed after him, the leader whose era had built it.

Under Gorbachev, Brezhnev's years became "the era of stagnation", and his name came off the map. On 6 January 1988 the city got its old name back, after barely five years. The truck works in the city still carry the old initials: KamAZ, the Kama Automobile Plant.

ja: 英領ベチュアナランド

states.question: Does the Cape Colony reach up to the Molopo River?

states.cue: The Cape reaches the Molopo River and the Bechuanaland Protectorate; no separate colony lies between them.

transitions.funFact: British Bechuanaland, the strip south of the Molopo River with Vryburg and Mafeking, was handed to the Cape Colony in November 1895. Mafeking, which also housed the protectorate's government, became famous four years later for surviving a 217-day Boer siege.

features.title: Kenya, Uganda and Tanganyika: British, or independent
features.subject: East Africa

states.label: Tanganyika German
states.question: Is the big territory south of Kenya German East Africa?
states.cue: South of British East Africa lies the large German colony, labelled German East Africa (Deutsch-Ostafrika) and in Germany's colour, reaching from Lake Victoria and Kilimanjaro to the Rovuma river.

states.label: All British
states.question: Are Kenya, Uganda and Tanganyika all British?
states.cue: All three share Britain's colour. Tanganyika, a former German colony, was run by Britain for the League of Nations and later the UN, so some maps add "Trust Territory".

states.label: Tanganyika independent
states.question: Is Tanganyika independent while Kenya and Uganda are still British?
states.cue: Tanganyika, the big territory south of Lake Victoria, has its own colour; Kenya and Uganda are still in Britain's.

states.label: Only Kenya British
states.question: Is Kenya the last British territory left in East Africa?
states.claim: Kenya is the last British land here
states.cue: Uganda and Tanganyika are independent; only Kenya still has Britain's colour.

states.label: All independent
states.question: Are Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania all independent?
states.claim: Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania are free
states.cue: Three separate countries with their own colours. South of Kenya the name is Tanzania, or Tanganyika on maps from 1961 to 1964.

transitions.funFact: German East Africa held out longer than any other German colony: its small army under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck was still fighting in November 1918 and only surrendered on 25 November, two weeks after the armistice in Europe. Britain then took most of the colony and named it Tanganyika Territory.

Tanganyika was the first of Britain's East African territories to become independent, on 9 December 1961. That night an army officer planted the new flag and a burning torch on the summit of Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, which until the First World War had stood in German East Africa.

Uganda became independent on 9 October 1962 with the old kingdom of Buganda inside it, and the Kabaka of Buganda became the country's first president a year later. Britain had run Uganda as a protectorate, not a settler colony, so it never had Kenya's large white farming community.

Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963, after the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s had made white settler rule untenable. Jomo Kenyatta, who had spent nine years in British prisons and detention, became its first prime minister. Kenyans celebrate the date as Jamhuri Day.

features.title: Gold Coast, Nigeria and Sierra Leone: British, or independent
features.subject: Gulf of Guinea

states.label: All British
states.question: Are the Gold Coast and Nigeria both British colonies?
states.claim: The Gold Coast and Nigeria are British
states.cue: Four British colonies along the coast: the Gambia, Sierra Leone, the Gold Coast and Nigeria, all in Britain's colour and often marked (Br.).

states.label: Ghana independent
states.question: Is Ghana independent while Nigeria is still British?
states.cue: Ghana (the former Gold Coast) has its own colour; Nigeria, Sierra Leone and the Gambia still share Britain's.

states.label: All independent
states.question: Are Ghana and Nigeria both independent countries?
states.cue: Ghana, Nigeria and Sierra Leone each have their own colour. Only the tiny Gambia stayed British until 1965.

transitions.funFact: The Gold Coast is often called the first colony south of the Sahara to win independence, on 6 March 1957. Its leader Kwame Nkrumah renamed it Ghana after a medieval West African empire, even though old Ghana lay hundreds of kilometres to the north-west, in today's Mauritania and Mali.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, became independent on 1 October 1960. Its name was coined in 1897 by the journalist Flora Shaw, later the wife of governor Frederick Lugard, after the Niger River. Sierra Leone followed in April 1961 and the tiny Gambia in 1965.

features.title: Brunei: British protectorate or independent sultanate

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Brunei an independent country, with no British mark?

states.label: British protectorate
states.question: Is Brunei a British protectorate?
states.cue: Brunei in British colour, or with (Br.) or "Brit. Prot." after the name. Until 1963 Sarawak and North Borneo around it are British too.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Brunei an independent country, with no British mark?
states.cue: Its own colour and plain name, without (Br.) or "British protectorate".

transitions.funFact: Once Brunei ruled most of Borneo's coast, but by the 1880s the "White Rajahs" of Sarawak and a British company in North Borneo had swallowed nearly all of it. To save what was left, the sultan accepted British protection in September 1888.

Oil found in 1929 made Brunei rich, and in 1963 its sultan refused to join Malaysia, shaken by a rebellion the year before and unwilling to share the revenue. It stayed a British protectorate for two more decades and became fully independent at midnight on New Year 1984.

features.title: Bulgaria's Aegean coast (Western Thrace)
features.subject: Bulgaria

states.label: No Aegean coast
states.question: Does Bulgaria stop short of the Aegean, with another country's land between it and the sea?
states.claim: Bulgaria stops short of the Aegean
states.cue: Bulgaria's southern border runs along the Rhodope mountains; the coast below is Turkish (before the Balkan Wars) or Greek (from 1920).

states.label: Bulgaria on the Aegean
states.question: Does Bulgaria reach the Aegean Sea, with a coast around Dedeagach?
states.cue: A strip of Bulgaria comes down to the Aegean between the Mesta and Maritsa rivers, with the port of Dedeagach (Dedeagatch, today Alexandroupoli).

states.label: No Aegean coast
states.question: Does Bulgaria stop short of the Aegean, with another country's land between it and the sea?
states.claim: Bulgaria stops short of the Aegean
states.cue: Western Thrace is Greek: Bulgaria ends in the Rhodope mountains.

states.label: Occupied (1941-44)
states.question: Does Bulgaria stop short of the Aegean, with another country's land between it and the sea?
states.claim: Bulgaria stops short of the Aegean
states.cue: Bulgaria occupies Greek Thrace and eastern Macedonia; Axis maps draw them as Bulgarian, all others keep the Greek border.

depictions.label: Bulgaria on the Aegean
depictions.question: Does Bulgaria reach the Aegean Sea, with a coast around Dedeagach?
depictions.cue: Axis-made maps draw the occupied coast as part of Bulgaria.

depictions.label: No Aegean coast
depictions.question: Does Bulgaria stop short of the Aegean, with another country's land between it and the sea?
depictions.claim: Bulgaria stops short of the Aegean
depictions.cue: The occupation is ignored: the Greek border stays.

states.label: No Aegean coast
states.question: Does Bulgaria stop short of the Aegean, with another country's land between it and the sea?
states.claim: Bulgaria stops short of the Aegean
states.cue: Back behind the Rhodope border; Bulgaria keeps southern Dobruja on the Black Sea.

transitions.funFact: Bulgaria fought its way to the Aegean in the First Balkan War, and even after losing the Second Balkan War to all its neighbours it kept a coastal strip between the Mesta and Maritsa rivers. Its only Aegean port was Dedeagach, a small railway town, today the Greek city of Alexandroupoli.

At Neuilly the victors took Bulgaria's Aegean coast. The treaty promised Bulgaria an economic outlet to the sea, which never really came. Greece took over in May 1920, and when King Alexander of Greece visited that summer, Dedeagach was renamed Alexandroupoli in his honour.

Bulgaria joined the Axis in March 1941, and after Germany crushed Greece its troops moved into western Thrace and eastern Macedonia, which Bulgaria declared part of the kingdom. Only Axis maps drew the new coast; for everyone else, the Greek border never moved.

When the Red Army reached Bulgaria in September 1944 the country switched sides, and the armistice signed in Moscow on 28 October sent its troops back behind the old border. The 1947 peace treaty confirmed it: Bulgaria kept southern Dobruja on the Black Sea, but never again reached the Aegean.

transitions.funFact: France carved the colony of Upper Volta out of Upper Senegal and Niger on 1 March 1919, naming it after the three branches of the Volta river, the Black, Red and White Volta, which rise there and flow south to Ghana.

In September 1932, to save money during the Depression, France abolished Upper Volta and shared its land between Ivory Coast, French Sudan and Niger. For fifteen years the country simply vanished from the map, until it was recreated in its old borders in 1947.

Mossi leaders campaigned for years to get their country back, and a French law of 4 September 1947 restored Upper Volta in its pre-1932 borders. It became an independent republic on 5 August 1960 under the same name.

On 4 August 1984, the first anniversary of his coup, the young president Thomas Sankara renamed Upper Volta Burkina Faso, 'land of upright people', combining words from Mooré and Dioula. He also gave the country a new flag and anthem, which he is said to have written himself.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Burma an independent country?
states.cue: Burma has its own colour, with the capital Rangoon; India is a separate independent country.

transitions.funFact: For half a century Burma was governed as a province of British India, conquered in three wars and completed with the annexation of Upper Burma on 1 January 1886. On 1 April 1937 Britain split it off as a separate colony with its own government in Rangoon.

After a Japanese occupation and a hard-fought Allied reconquest, Burma became independent on 4 January 1948, months after India and Pakistan. Unlike them it chose not to join the Commonwealth, and Rangoon remained its capital until 2005.

transitions.funFact: In March 1970, while Prince Sihanouk was abroad, General Lon Nol seized power, and on 9 October 1970 he abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the Khmer Republic. The country was dragged into the Vietnam War, and US bombing of its eastern provinces intensified.

The Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975 and declared 'Year Zero', emptying the cities. Their state, Democratic Kampuchea, used the Khmer pronunciation of the country's name. After Vietnam drove them out in 1979, the new government kept the name as the People's Republic of Kampuchea.

As Vietnamese troops prepared to leave, the government renamed the country the State of Cambodia on 30 April 1989, dropping the name associated with the Khmer Rouge years. The monarchy, under Sihanouk again, came back in 1993.

states.cue: The Caprivi Strip (Caprivizipfel), 30 to 100 km wide, runs east between Angola and Northern Rhodesia to the north and Bechuanaland to the south, reaching the Zambezi upstream of Victoria Falls.

transitions.funFact: In the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty Germany gave up its claims to Zanzibar for the North Sea island of Heligoland and a thin finger of land reaching from South West Africa to the Zambezi, named after Chancellor Leo von Caprivi. The idea was a river route east towards German East Africa, but Victoria Falls and the gorges below it block every boat.

transitions.funFact: Ubangi-Shari was named after its two great rivers, the Ubangi on its southern border and the Shari flowing north to Lake Chad. Its leader Barthélemy Boganda chose "Central African Republic" in 1958, hoping it would grow into a larger union of former French colonies. It never did.

President Jean-Bédel Bokassa admired Napoleon so much that he declared himself emperor on 4 December 1976 and renamed the country the Central African Empire. His coronation a year later, on a throne shaped like an eagle, cost about a third of the national budget.

After Bokassa's troops killed schoolchildren who had protested against compulsory uniforms, France lost patience. While he was visiting Libya in September 1979, French paratroopers flew in, put his predecessor David Dacko back in power and restored the Central African Republic.

features.title: Name of the island country south-east of India

states.label: Sri Lanka

states.cue: The country has been called Sri Lanka since 1972.

transitions.funFact: Ceylon won independence from Britain in 1948 but kept its colonial name until 22 May 1972, when a new constitution created the Republic of Sri Lanka. Lanka is the island's name in ancient Sanskrit epics, and Sri is an honorific meaning roughly 'resplendent'. The tea is still sold as Ceylon tea.

features.subject: Bolivia and Paraguay

states.cue: Paraguay is twice its old size: a fixed border runs across the Chaco far to the west and north, and Bolivia is shut off from the Paraguay river except for a short stretch.

transitions.funFact: Bolivia and Paraguay fought the bloody Chaco War of 1932-35 over a dry wilderness believed to hold oil. Paraguay won about three quarters of the disputed land, fixed by an award in October 1938. No oil was found there at the time; Paraguay announced finds only in 2012.

transitions.funFact: On 10 May 1953 East Germany renamed Chemnitz, an industrial city that had lost much of its centre to wartime bombing, Karl-Marx-Stadt, for the 135th anniversary of Marx's birth. A 7-metre bronze head of Marx, nicknamed the "Nischel", still stands in the city centre.

In April 1990, months before German reunification, 76 per cent of voters in a citizens' poll chose the old name, and Karl-Marx-Stadt became Chemnitz again on 1 June 1990. Czech maps call the city Saská Kamenice, "Saxon Kamenice", so on Czech globes it looks different again.

states.cue: The star sits at Peking (Beijing on newer maps), capital of the People's Republic.

transitions.funFact: Chiang Kai-shek took Nanking in 1927 and made it the Nationalist capital, and when the northern government in Peking fell in 1928 the capital star moved south. Peking, "northern capital", was renamed Peiping, "northern peace", to make the point.

As Japanese armies closed in on Nanking in late 1937, the government fled up the Yangtze to Chungking, behind the gorges. For eight years the river city was China's wartime capital, bombed again and again from 1938 to 1943.

In May 1946, nine months after Japan's surrender, the government moved back to Nanking. The return lasted only three years: the Communists took the city in April 1949, and the Nationalists ended up in Taipei.

Days before Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949, the new government made the northern city its capital again and restored its name. The capital star has stayed in Peking, now spelled Beijing, ever since.

transitions.funFact: The pilot Valery Chkalov, famous for flying non-stop from Moscow over the North Pole to the United States in 1937, died in a test crash in December 1938. Days later Orenburg was named after him, although he was not born there, never lived there and never visited.

On 4 December 1957 the city got its old name back, in a wave of renamings after Stalin's death. A month earlier a cadet named Yuri Gagarin had graduated from its air force pilots' school; the city keeps a memorial flat of Yuri and Valentina Gagarin, and its airport now bears his name.

transitions.funFact: Soviet surveyors in the Pamirs at first thought the highest peak in the USSR was the known Mount Garmo. By 1932 they had shown it was a different mountain, 7,495 metres high, and in 1933 it was named Stalin Peak. Yevgeny Abalakov climbed it that same year.

In 1962 Stalin Peak became Communism Peak, still the highest point of the Soviet Union. Climbers who conquered all five Soviet peaks over 7,000 metres earned the title Snow Leopard, and Communism Peak was the hardest of them.

Independent Tajikistan dropped Communism Peak in 1998 for Ismoil Somoni Peak, after the Samanid emir Ismail Samani, who died in 907 and whose name is also on the currency, the somoni. Many climbing maps still print Pik Kommunizma.

states.question: Is the Congo a 'Free State'?

states.question: Is Congo an independent country?
states.cue: It has its own colour with no link to Belgium. Depending on the year it's called Congo, Congo-Léopoldville, Zaire or DR Congo.

transitions.funFact: The Congo Free State was the personal property of King Leopold II, not of Belgium. After an international outcry over forced labour and atrocities in the rubber trade, the Belgian state took it over as a colony on 15 November 1908.

Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960, during the 'Year of Africa' in which seventeen African countries gained independence. On many maps half the continent changes colour around 1960, so the colonial palette is one of the quickest ways to place a map before or after.

transitions.funFact: King Leopold II ran the Congo Free State as his personal property, and reports of forced labour and mutilation on rubber plantations caused an international outcry. On 15 November 1908 the Belgian state took the colony over, and it became the Belgian Congo, eighty times the size of Belgium.

The Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 as the Republic of the Congo, the same name as its neighbour across the river, so maps added the capitals: Congo (Léopoldville) and Congo (Brazzaville). Within weeks the new country was torn by mutinies and the secession of Katanga.

On 27 October 1971 President Mobutu renamed the country, the river and the currency Zaire, from a Portuguese version of a Kongo word for river. Citizens had to drop Christian names, and Mobutu himself became Mobutu Sese Seko Kuku Ngbendu Wa Za Banga.

Rebels led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila swept across the country in seven months and entered Kinshasa on 17 May 1997. Mobutu fled after 32 years in power, and Kabila immediately restored the name Democratic Republic of the Congo, which the country had used from 1964 to 1971.

transitions.funFact: Crimea had been moved from the Russian to the Ukrainian Soviet republic on 19 February 1954, which mattered little while both were part of the USSR. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991 that internal line became an international border, and Crimea, with Russia's Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol, ended up in Ukraine.

In February 2014 soldiers without insignia seized Crimea's parliament and airports. After a hastily organised referendum that most countries rejected, Russia annexed the peninsula on 18 March 2014. A 19-kilometre road and rail bridge across the Kerch Strait, the longest in Europe, opened in 2018.

Its constitution balanced Greeks and Turks so carefully that it broke down within three years, and Britain kept two sovereign military bases on the island, still marked on detailed maps.

After a coup backed by the Greek junta tried to unite Cyprus with Greece, Turkey invaded on 20 July 1974 and took the northern 37 per cent of the island. The ceasefire line still splits Nicosia, the last divided capital in Europe, and UN troops patrol it.

features.subject: Country around Prague

states.label: Austria-Hungary

states.cue: Before 1918 Bohemia and Moravia belong to Austria-Hungary, whose name runs across central Europe.

states.label: Czechoslovakia
states.question: Is the country around Prague called {name}?
states.cue: Czechoslovakia, the long country from Bohemia to the Carpathians, 1918-1992.

states.label: Czech Republic
states.question: Is the country around Prague called {name}?
states.cue: The Czech Republic, the western part of former Czechoslovakia, from 1993.

states.label: Czechia
states.question: Is the country around Prague called {name}?
states.cue: Czechia, the official short name since 2016. German, Dutch, Russian and Polish maps had used a one-word name all along.

transitions.funFact: On 28 October 1918, as Austria-Hungary fell apart at the end of the First World War, the National Committee in Prague proclaimed an independent Czechoslovak state that joined the Czech lands with Slovakia. Its first president, Tomáš Masaryk, had spent the war abroad winning over the Allies.

Czechoslovakia split peacefully at midnight on 1 January 1993, without a referendum, after Czech and Slovak leaders failed to agree on a looser federation. People called it the Velvet Divorce, after the Velvet Revolution of 1989 that had ended communist rule.

In 2016 the Czech government chose Czechia as the official short name in English, so the country no longer needs a two-word name on maps and sports kits. The United Nations added it to its databases that July, but adoption has been slow and many maps still print Czech Republic.

features.title: Czechoslovakia: interwar, cut down at Munich, broken up, post-war, or two countries
features.subject: Czechoslovakia

states.label: Part of Austria-Hungary
states.question: Are Bohemia and Slovakia part of Austria-Hungary?
states.cue: No Czechoslovakia: Bohemia and Moravia belong to Austria, Slovakia and Ruthenia to Hungary, all inside Austria-Hungary.

ja: オーストリア＝ハンガリー

states.cue: A long country from the Bohemian hills to Ruthenia in the far east, where it borders Poland and Romania.

states.label: Cut down at Munich
states.question: Has Czechoslovakia lost its rim to Germany and a southern strip to Hungary?
states.cue: Germany has taken the Sudeten rim around Bohemia, so Czechoslovakia is thin and ragged; Hungary has a strip of southern Slovakia. Only on maps of late 1938 and early 1939.

states.label: Broken up (1939–45)
states.question: Are Bohemia and Moravia part of Germany, with Slovakia on its own?
states.claim: Bohemia is German, Slovakia on its own
states.cue: No Czechoslovakia: Bohemia and Moravia share Germany's colour as a protectorate, Slovakia is a separate state, and Hungary holds Ruthenia.

depictions.label: Protectorate and Slovakia
depictions.question: Are Bohemia and Moravia part of Germany, with Slovakia on its own?
depictions.claim: Bohemia is German, Slovakia on its own
depictions.cue: Bohemia and Moravia in German colour, Slovakia separate.

depictions.label: Pre-Munich Czechoslovakia
depictions.question: Does Czechoslovakia stretch from Bohemia to a tail touching Romania?
depictions.claim: Czechoslovakia has a tail to Romania
depictions.cue: Some Allied maps kept Czechoslovakia in its 1937 borders, as the exile government claimed.

states.label: Post-war, without the eastern tail
states.question: Is Czechoslovakia one country that ends at the Ukrainian border, without a tail?
states.claim: Czechoslovakia has lost its eastern tail
states.cue: Czechoslovakia is back, but Ruthenia, the tail in the east, is now Soviet, so it no longer touches Romania.

states.label: Two countries
states.question: Are there two countries, the Czech Republic and Slovakia?
states.claim: The Czech Republic and Slovakia are split
states.cue: A border runs between Moravia and Slovakia: Czech Republic (Czechia) with Prague, Slovakia with Bratislava.

transitions.funFact: Czechoslovakia was born in Prague on 28 October 1918, as Austria-Hungary fell apart. The peace treaties added Ruthenia at the far eastern end, giving the new state a long, thin shape and, oddly, a border with Romania.

At Munich, Britain and France agreed that Germany could take the Sudetenland, the German-speaking rim of Bohemia, without asking the Czechoslovaks. German troops crossed on 1 October 1938, and the country lost its border mountains and fortifications.

Less than six months after Munich, Germany occupied the rest of the Czech lands. Slovakia declared itself independent the day before, Hungary marched into Ruthenia, and Hitler proclaimed the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia from Prague Castle.

Czechoslovakia came back in 1945, but not whole: in June it signed Ruthenia over to the Soviet Union, which joined it to Soviet Ukraine. The eastern tail that had touched Romania disappeared, and with it the Czechoslovak-Romanian border.

At midnight on 1 January 1993 Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia, the so-called Velvet Divorce. No referendum was held: the two governments agreed it, and the new border followed the old line between Moravia and Slovakia.

states.cue: Poland's colour runs along the whole coast here; the city is printed as Gdańsk, often with (Danzig).

transitions.funFact: The Treaty of Versailles turned Danzig into a Free City under the League of Nations: a mini-state of about 1,966 km² with its own currency, the gulden, and stamps, while Poland ran its port, railways and post. It sat awkwardly between the Polish corridor and Germany.

The first shots of the Second World War were fired here: at 4:45 on 1 September 1939 the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte, in the Free City's harbour. Germany annexed the Free City the same day.

Soviet and Polish troops took the ruined city in March 1945, and the Potsdam conference gave it to Poland. Most German inhabitants were expelled, and as Gdańsk it later became the birthplace of Solidarity, the trade union that helped end communist rule.

transitions.funFact: Kiribati's islands are scattered across almost 4,000 km of ocean, and until 1994 the date line ran through the middle of the country, so offices on either side shared only four working days a week. President Teburoro Tito moved the whole country to the Asian side, and the eastern islands skipped 31 December 1994.

Samoa had been on the American side of the line since 1892, when traders persuaded its king to align with California. In 2011, with Australia and New Zealand as its main partners, it switched back: Thursday 29 December was followed by Saturday 31 December, and Friday 30 December never happened there.

Fretilin declared independence on 28 November 1975; nine days later Indonesia invaded, and in July 1976 it declared the territory its 27th province. The United Nations never accepted the annexation.

In a UN-run vote on 30 August 1999, 78.5% of East Timorese chose independence, and pro-Indonesian militias answered by burning much of the country. After two and a half years under UN administration, Timor-Leste became the first new sovereign state of the 21st century on 20 May 2002.

features.subject: Eritrea

states.claim: Italy holds a few posts on the coast
states.cue: Small Italian holdings on the coast, around Assab and Massawa, labelled Assab (It.), Massaua or Italian possessions; the highlands around Asmara are still Abyssinian, and the name Eritrea is missing.

states.label: Italian colony on the coast
states.question: Is Eritrea an Italian colony?
states.cue: A narrow strip along the Red Sea in Italy's colour, or labelled Eritrea (It.) or Colonia Eritrea. Ethiopia (Abyssinia) is a separate country inland.

states.label: All Italian East Africa
states.question: Is Eritrea part of one big Italian East Africa?
states.claim: Eritrea is in Italian East Africa
states.cue: Eritrea, Ethiopia and Italian Somaliland are one Italian territory, labelled Italian East Africa, Africa Orientale Italiana or A.O.I. Only on maps from 1936 to about 1941.

ja: イタリア領東アフリカ

states.label: Separate territory, British-run
states.question: Is Eritrea run by the British?
states.claim: Eritrea is run by the British
states.cue: Eritrea is still separate from Ethiopia but no longer Italian: British colour, or (Br.) or 'Br. Adm.' after its name. Typical of maps from the 1940s.

states.label: Autonomous part of Ethiopia
states.question: Is Eritrea an autonomous part of Ethiopia?
states.claim: Eritrea is an autonomous part of Ethiopia
states.cue: Eritrea is in Ethiopia's colour but keeps its own outline, often dashed, with its name in smaller type.

states.label: No Eritrea

states.cue: There's no Eritrea: Ethiopia reaches the Red Sea. At most a small province name remains.

states.label: Independent Eritrea
states.question: Is Eritrea an independent country?
states.cue: Eritrea has its own colour and a capital star at Asmara. Ethiopia has no coastline.

transitions.funFact: Italy bought the port of Assab through a shipping company in 1869 and took Massawa in 1885. After occupying the highlands around Asmara in 1889, it united everything into one colony on 1 January 1890. The diplomat Carlo Dossi suggested the name Eritrea, from the ancient Greek name of the Red Sea, instead of "New Ethiopia".

Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935 and captured Addis Ababa in May 1936. On 1 June 1936 Rome merged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Italian Somaliland into a single colony, Italian East Africa, so for five years Ethiopia disappeared from many maps.

British and Commonwealth troops, together with Ethiopian fighters, defeated the Italians in East Africa in 1941. Emperor Haile Selassie returned to Addis Ababa, but Eritrea stayed under British military administration while the new United Nations debated its future.

A 1950 United Nations resolution made Eritrea an autonomous unit federated with Ethiopia, with its own parliament and flag. The federation started on 15 September 1952, the day the British administration handed over power and left.

Emperor Haile Selassie steadily hollowed out Eritrea's autonomy, and on 14 November 1962 its assembly, under heavy pressure, voted to dissolve the federation. Eritrea became Ethiopia's fourteenth province, which helped fuel a thirty-year war of independence.

Eritrean fighters took Asmara in May 1991, but formal independence followed only after a UN-monitored referendum in April 1993, in which 99.8 percent voted yes. Independence on 24 May 1993 left Ethiopia without a coastline, which is easy to spot on any map.

states.claim: Abyssinia is a small highland empire
states.cue: Abyssinia in its own colour around the northern and central highlands; the lands to the south and east are left blank or carry tribal names such as Galla and Somali.

states.cue: An independent Ethiopia (Abyssinia) in its own colour from Eritrea's border south to the north end of Lake Rudolf and east into the Ogaden, ringed by British, French and Italian colonies.

ja: イタリア領東アフリカ

states.label: Large independent empire
states.question: Is Abyssinia a large independent empire, reaching south to Lake Rudolf and east into the Ogaden?
states.cue: An independent Ethiopia in its own colour from the Red Sea hills south to Lake Rudolf and east into the Ogaden.

transitions.funFact: The Treaty of Wuchale of May 1889 came in two languages. In Amharic, Article 17 said Emperor Menelik could use Italy for his foreign affairs; in Italian, it said he must. Italy announced a protectorate over Ethiopia that October, Britain accepted Abyssinia as Italy's sphere in 1891, and European maps began to colour it Italian.

Menelik rejected the Italian reading of the treaty and bought modern rifles. At Adwa on 1 March 1896 his army crushed an Italian invasion force, killing over 6,000 Italian and colonial soldiers, the worst defeat of a colonial army in Africa. In the Treaty of Addis Ababa that October Italy dropped the protectorate and recognised Ethiopia as fully independent.

Ethiopia grew while Europe carved up Africa around it. Menelik's armies had conquered the south and east in the 1880s and 1890s, and after Adwa the colonial powers came to Addis Ababa to agree borders, starting with Britain's envoy Rennell Rodd in May 1897. By 1908 Ethiopia reached Lake Rudolf and deep into the Ogaden.

Mussolini avenged Adwa forty years later. Italian armies, using poison gas, took Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, and four days later Italy declared Ethiopia annexed, with King Victor Emmanuel III as its emperor. On 1 June it was merged with Eritrea and Italian Somaliland into Italian East Africa, and Ethiopia vanished from the map.

British, Commonwealth and Ethiopian forces broke up Italian East Africa in 1941. Emperor Haile Selassie rode back into Addis Ababa on 5 May 1941, five years to the day after the Italians had marched in, and Ethiopia returned to the map in its pre-war borders. The last Italian army held out at Gondar until November.

states.claim: Finland ends short of the Arctic Ocean
states.cue: Finland has no Arctic coast: Norway and Russia meet in the far north. Viipuri (Vyborg) and Lake Ladoga are in Russia.

transitions.funFact: Finland declared independence from Russia on 6 December 1917, weeks after the Bolshevik revolution. In the 1920 Treaty of Tartu Soviet Russia also ceded Petsamo, a strip of tundra that gave Finland an ice-free Arctic harbour at Liinahamari, and soon after nickel was found there.

The Winter War ended with the Moscow Peace of March 1940. Finland gave up about 9 percent of its land, including its second city Viipuri and the shores of Lake Ladoga, but kept Petsamo, which the Red Army had occupied and handed back.

The 1944 armistice that ended the Continuation War took Petsamo too, so Finland lost its Arctic coast and nickel mines, and Norway and the Soviet Union became neighbours. Finland also had to lease the Porkkala peninsula near Helsinki to the Soviets, until 1956.

states.cue: Guinea, on the coast south of Senegal, has its own colour; everything around it is still French. This lasted less than two years.

transitions.funFact: In September 1958 de Gaulle let every French African colony vote on joining a new French Community. Only Guinea said no, by 95 per cent. It became independent four days later, on 2 October, and France left so abruptly that departing officials reportedly took files, furniture and even telephones with them.

1960 was the Year of Africa: fourteen French colonies and trust territories became independent within eleven months, eight of them in just seventeen days of August. Globe makers had to repaint more than a quarter of the continent, which is why maps from 1959 and 1961 look so different.

features.subject: North-west Africa

states.label: Morocco independent
states.question: Is Morocco an independent sultanate, while Algeria and Tunisia share France's colour?
states.cue: Algeria and Tunisia are coloured like France, but Morocco has a colour of its own as the Sultanate of Morocco (Empire chérifien, Marokko).

states.label: All three French
states.question: Are Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia all coloured like France?
states.cue: All three share France's colour: Morocco and Tunisia as protectorates, Algeria as part of France itself. A strip along Morocco's north coast is Spanish (Spanish Morocco), and Tangier is an international zone.

states.label: Only Algeria French
states.question: Is Algeria still French while Morocco and Tunisia are independent?
states.claim: Algeria is French, the others free
states.cue: Morocco and Tunisia have their own colours, but Algeria still shares France's. French maps of the time divide Algeria into départements like France's own.

states.label: All independent
states.question: Are Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia all independent countries?
states.cue: Three separate colours, none of them France's. Algeria is by far the biggest of the three.

transitions.funFact: Morocco was the last independent country in North Africa. After the 1911 Agadir Crisis Germany stepped aside in return for land in Central Africa, and on 30 March 1912 Sultan Abd al-Hafid signed the Treaty of Fez under heavy pressure. France took most of the country; Spain got the Rif coast and the far south in November.

France gave up its protectorates over Morocco and Tunisia within three weeks in March 1956, and Spain handed back its northern strip of Morocco in April. Algeria was different: France ruled it as part of France itself, home to about a million European settlers, so it stayed French for six more years.

After eight years of war, Algerians voted almost unanimously for independence on 1 July 1962, and the country declared it on 5 July, exactly 132 years after the French had taken Algiers in 1830. Nearly a million settlers, the pieds-noirs, left for France within months.
