states.label: Danzig
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Danzig (Dantzig, Danzica), the German name.

states.label: Gdańsk
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Gdańsk (Gdansk, Гданьск), the Polish name; often with (Danzig) in brackets.

transitions.funFact: The war began here, with the shelling of Westerplatte on 1 September 1939, and the city was taken by Soviet and Polish troops in March 1945. Its German population was expelled, and as Gdańsk the city later gave birth to Solidarity in its shipyard in 1980.

features.title: Name of Georgia on Japanese maps
features.subject: Country south of the Caucasus

states.label: Gurujia
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: グルジア (Gurujia), from the Russian name Грузия, on Japanese maps until 2015.

states.label: Jōjia
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: ジョージア (Jōjia), from the English Georgia, on Japanese maps since April 2015.

transitions.funFact: Japan long called the country Gurujia, after the Russian name. After its 2008 war with Russia, Georgia asked the world to drop Russian-style names. Japan said no in 2011, but when Georgia’s president raised it again with Prime Minister Abe in 2015, Japan agreed: maps now say Jōjia, from the English Georgia.

sources.title: Embassy of Japan in Georgia: the Japanese name of Georgia changed to Jōjia on 22 April 2015

features.title: Germany's outline and number of German states
features.subject: Germany

states.label: German Empire
states.question: Is Germany the large German Empire?
states.cue: Germany includes Alsace-Lorraine in the west and runs along the Baltic to Memel in the east. There's no Poland: Germany borders Russia directly.

states.label: Interwar Germany
states.question: Is East Prussia cut off from the rest of Germany?
states.claim: East Prussia is cut off from Germany
states.cue: A Polish corridor reaches the Baltic Sea near Danzig and splits East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Austria and Czechoslovakia are separate countries.

states.label: Greater Germany
states.question: Does Germany include Austria?
states.cue: There's no Austria: Germany runs down to Italy and usually takes in the rim of Czechoslovakia (the Sudetenland). Often labelled Deutsches Reich or Grossdeutschland.

states.label: Occupied post-war Germany
states.question: Is Germany one country in its smaller post-war shape?
states.claim: Germany is one, in its post-war shape
states.cue: Germany ends at the Oder and Neisse rivers, close to today's outline, but isn't split into two states yet. Thin lines may mark the four occupation zones.

states.label: Two German states
states.question: Are there two German states?
states.cue: West Germany and East Germany are separate countries: look for BRD and DDR, FRG and GDR, or RFA and RDA. West Berlin is an island inside the East.

states.label: Reunified Germany
states.question: Is Germany one reunified country?
states.cue: One Germany in today's outline, with Berlin inside it as the capital and no border through the middle.

transitions.funFact: The Treaty of Versailles came into force on 10 January 1920 and took away roughly an eighth of Germany's territory. Alsace-Lorraine went back to France, and a corridor gave the new Poland access to the sea, leaving East Prussia stranded as a German island on the Baltic coast.

German troops crossed into Austria on 12 March 1938, and the next day Austria was declared part of the Reich. The Anschluss wiped Austria off the map for seven years; that autumn the Munich Agreement also handed the Sudetenland border region of Czechoslovakia to Germany.

Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945. At Potsdam that summer the Allies put the lands east of the Oder and Neisse rivers under Polish and Soviet administration, so Silesia, Pomerania and East Prussia vanished from Germany, and what remained was divided into four occupation zones.

In 1949 the occupation zones hardened into two states: the Federal Republic in the west, founded in May, and the German Democratic Republic in the east, founded on 7 October. For four decades most maps showed two Germanys, with West Berlin as an island inside the East.

Less than a year after the Berlin Wall fell, East Germany joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. Maps printed in the months before often still showed two states, which makes Germany one of the sharpest clues for globes made around 1990.

lookalikes.note: One Germany in nearly today's outline, 1945-49 and after 1990

features.title: Gold Coast or Ghana
features.subject: Coast west of Nigeria

states.label: Gold Coast
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: A British colony, often printed Gold Coast (Br.), Goudkust, Goldküste or Côte-de-l'Or.

states.label: Ghana
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Independent since 1957 under the name Ghana.

transitions.funFact: Kwame Nkrumah chose the name Ghana to link the new state to a rich medieval empire famous for its gold, although old Ghana lay far to the north-west. The colonial name Gold Coast came from the European traders who bought gold along this shore from the 15th century on.

features.title: Location of Burundi's capital
features.subject: Burundi's capital

states.label: Capital on the lake
states.question: Is the capital Bujumbura, on Lake Tanganyika?
states.cue: The capital symbol sits at Bujumbura (Usumbura until 1962) on the north-east shore of Lake Tanganyika.

states.label: Capital in the hills
states.question: Is the capital Gitega, in the middle of the country?
states.cue: The star is at Gitega in the central highlands; Bujumbura is shown as an ordinary city.

transitions.funFact: In December 2018 Burundi's government made Gitega, a hill town of around 30,000 people and once the seat of Burundi's kings, the political capital. Bujumbura, on Lake Tanganyika, stayed the economic capital and the biggest city by far, and many ministries took years to move.

features.title: Name of the port on Algoa Bay, South Africa
features.subject: Port on Algoa Bay

states.label: Port Elizabeth
states.question: Is the port called {name}?
states.cue: Port Elizabeth (Pt. Elizabeth), the name since 1820.

states.label: Gqeberha
states.question: Is the port called {name}?
states.cue: Gqeberha, the isiXhosa name of the river through the city, official since February 2021.

transitions.funFact: Port Elizabeth was named in 1820 by the Cape's acting governor after his wife Elizabeth, who had died in India two years before. Since 2021 the city is Gqeberha, the isiXhosa name of the Baakens River, and its first sound is a click, made by snapping the tongue off the roof of the mouth.

sources.title: It is official: Port Elizabeth has a new name, Gqeberha (TimesLIVE, 23 February 2021)

features.title: Canton or Guangzhou
features.subject: City on the Pearl River

states.label: Canton
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Canton (Kanton, Cantón, Cantão).

states.label: Guangzhou
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Guangzhou, the Pinyin spelling, in English, German, Dutch and Scandinavian maps.

transitions.funFact: Canton is an old European rendering of the province's name, Guangdong; the city itself is Guangzhou in Pinyin. China asked the world to use Pinyin from 1979. English, German and Dutch maps switched, but French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Polish and Czech maps still say Canton.

features.title: The three Guianas: colonies, or Guyana and Suriname
features.subject: The Guianas

states.label: Three colonies
states.question: Are all three Guianas still colonies (British, Dutch and French)?
states.cue: Three colonies side by side, each in its ruler's colour: British Guiana, Dutch Guiana (Surinam) and French Guiana.

states.label: Guyana independent
states.question: Is Guyana independent while Suriname and French Guiana are still colonies?
states.claim: Guyana is independent, the rest colonies
states.cue: The westernmost, Guyana, has its own colour; Surinam is still Dutch and French Guiana French.

states.label: Only French Guiana
states.question: Are Guyana and Suriname independent, with only French Guiana left?
states.claim: Only French Guiana is a colony
states.cue: Only French Guiana keeps a European colour. It is part of France itself, so many maps colour it like France.

transitions.funFact: British Guiana became independent as Guyana on 26 May 1966. It is the only English-speaking country in South America, where cricket is bigger than football. Venezuela claims about two-thirds of it, and Venezuelan maps hatch everything west of the Essequibo River as a "zone in reclamation".

Suriname became independent from the Netherlands on 25 November 1975, and around a third of its people moved to the Netherlands in the years around it. The Dutch had kept this colony in 1667 in exchange for New Amsterdam, the future New York, which went to England.

features.title: Name of the gulf between the United States, Mexico and Cuba
features.subject: Gulf south of the United States

states.label: Gulf of Mexico
states.question: Is the gulf called {name}, with no other name printed in it?
states.cue: Gulf of Mexico across the whole gulf, the name on maps for centuries and still the international name.

states.label: Gulf of America
states.question: Does your map print {name} in the gulf?
states.cue: Gulf of America on US-made maps since 2025, sometimes as a second name near the US coast with Gulf of Mexico further out.

depictions.label: Gulf of America
depictions.question: Does your map print Gulf of America in the gulf?
depictions.claim: The gulf is called Gulf of America
depictions.cue: US government maps, some US globe makers and National Geographic (near the US coast) print Gulf of America.

depictions.label: Gulf of Mexico kept
depictions.question: Is the gulf still called Gulf of Mexico only?
depictions.cue: Maps made outside the US, and many US maps, keep Gulf of Mexico.

transitions.funFact: On his first day back in office, President Trump ordered the US part of the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America. Google Maps now shows Americans one name, Mexicans the other, and everyone else both. The Associated Press kept the old name and was barred from the Oval Office for it.

sources.title: Interior Department implements 'Gulf of America' and 'Mount McKinley' name changes (24 January 2025)

features.title: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Trucial States: British, or independent
features.subject: Persian Gulf coast

states.label: No Qatar yet
states.question: Is Qatar without a border of its own?
states.claim: Qatar is part of Ottoman Arabia
states.cue: The Qatar peninsula is part of Ottoman Arabia, often uncoloured, with no border of its own; the Trucial Coast to the east is marked British.

states.label: All British
states.question: Are Kuwait, Qatar and the Trucial States all British protectorates?
states.claim: Kuwait, Qatar and Trucial States British
states.cue: The small sheikhdoms along the Gulf (Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Trucial States, also called Trucial Oman) are in Britain's colour or marked (Br.).

states.label: Kuwait independent
states.question: Is Kuwait independent while Qatar and the Trucial States are still British?
states.claim: Kuwait is independent, the rest British
states.cue: Kuwait at the head of the Gulf has its own colour; the sheikhdoms further south are still Britain's.

states.label: UAE exists
states.question: Is there a country called the United Arab Emirates?
states.claim: There is a United Arab Emirates
states.cue: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (U.A.E.) are all separate countries with their own colours.

transitions.funFact: Qatar was an Ottoman outpost until the Turkish garrison left Doha in 1915. A year later its sheikh signed a treaty handing foreign affairs and protection to Britain, and maps gave the peninsula a border of its own. Its oil and gas wealth came decades later.

Kuwait ended its British protection treaty on 19 June 1961. Six days later Iraq claimed it as a lost province, and Britain rushed troops back to defend it. Kuwait was already one of the world's great oil exporters, and Iraq's claim returned with its invasion in 1990.

When Britain decided to withdraw from everything east of Suez, the Gulf sheikhdoms had to go it alone. Bahrain and Qatar chose independence in 1971, and six Trucial States, once the Pirate Coast of British charts, federated as the United Arab Emirates on 2 December. Ras al-Khaimah joined two months later.

features.title: Hainan: part of Guangdong, or its own province
features.subject: South China coast

states.label: Part of Guangdong
states.question: Is Hainan island in the same colour as Guangdong, as part of that province?
states.cue: The island shares Guangdong's colour, and the province name Guangdong (Kwangtung, Canton) covers both.

states.label: Own province
states.question: Is Hainan island a province of its own, in its own colour?
states.claim: Hainan is a province of its own
states.cue: Hainan has its own colour and name, with Haikou as its capital; Guangdong stops at the Leizhou peninsula.

transitions.funFact: Hainan, an island about the size of Belgium, had been governed from Guangzhou for centuries. In April 1988 Deng Xiaoping's reformers made it China's newest province and, at the same moment, the country's largest special economic zone, open to foreign investors.

features.title: Sea border around Hans Island in Nares Strait
features.subject: Nares Strait

states.label: No sea border
states.question: Is there no border line at all through the strait between Greenland and Ellesmere Island?
states.claim: No border runs through the strait
states.cue: Before 1973 no boundary is drawn between Greenland and Canada's Arctic islands.

states.label: Border with a gap
states.question: Does the sea border run up the strait but stop short around Hans Island?
states.claim: The sea border stops at Hans Island
states.cue: From 1973 a line runs down the middle of the strait, interrupted around Hans Island, which both countries claimed.

states.label: Border across the island
states.question: Does the sea border run straight through the strait and across Hans Island?
states.claim: The border runs across Hans Island
states.cue: Since 2022 the line is continuous and crosses Hans Island itself: Canada's only land border with a European country.

transitions.funFact: In December 1973 Canada and Denmark agreed a seabed boundary down the middle of the waters between Greenland and Canada's Arctic islands. They could not agree who owned Hans Island, a bare rock in the middle of Nares Strait, so they simply left a gap in the line around it.

For almost 50 years Canada and Denmark both claimed Hans Island. Officials visiting the rock planted their flag and left a bottle of Canadian whisky or Danish schnapps for the other side, a ritual nicknamed the Whisky War. On 14 June 2022 they split the island roughly in half, creating a land border.

features.title: Name of Zimbabwe's capital
features.subject: Capital of Zimbabwe

states.label: Salisbury
states.question: Is the capital called {name}?
states.cue: Salisbury, after the British prime minister Lord Salisbury, from 1890.

states.label: Harare
states.question: Is the capital called {name}?
states.cue: Harare, after a local Shona chief, since 1982.

transitions.funFact: The town grew from Fort Salisbury, founded in 1890 by Rhodes's Pioneer Column and named after the British prime minister. On 18 April 1982, the second anniversary of independence, it became Harare, after Neharawa, a Shona chief whose people lived on a nearby hill.

features.title: Hatay (Alexandretta): Ottoman, Syrian, or Turkish
features.subject: Syria and Turkey

states.label: Ottoman, no border
states.question: Is there no border here, with Syria and Anatolia both Turkish?
states.claim: Syria and Anatolia are both Ottoman
states.cue: One Ottoman (Turkish) colour from Anatolia down through Syria; no border crosses the region.

states.label: Syrian (Sanjak of Alexandretta)
states.question: Do Antioch and Alexandretta lie inside Syria?
states.cue: Syria's border runs up to the Gulf of Alexandretta; Antioch (Antakya) and Alexandretta are Syrian, often in French mandate colour, sometimes with a sanjak boundary.

states.label: Turkish (Hatay)
states.question: Are Antioch and Alexandretta inside Turkey?
states.cue: Turkey's colour reaches down the coast past Antakya (Antioch) and İskenderun; Syria's border meets the sea further south. Syrian maps still show the corner as Syrian.

transitions.funFact: After the Ottoman defeat, France took Syria as a League of Nations mandate. A 1921 treaty with the Turkish nationalists left the Sanjak of Alexandretta, with its Turkish, Arab and Armenian population, inside Syria but with special autonomy.

In 1938 the sanjak became the Hatay State, a name Atatürk's government coined after the ancient Hittites. Ten months later its assembly voted to join Turkey, while France, hoping to keep Turkey out of Hitler's camp, looked away. Syria never accepted the loss.

features.title: Hawaii: independent kingdom or republic, or annexed by the United States
features.subject: North Pacific

states.label: Independent Hawaii
states.question: Is Hawaii an independent country, not in the colour of the United States?
states.cue: The islands in a colour of their own, labelled Hawaii, Hawaiian Islands or Sandwich Islands (Sandwich-Inseln, Îles Sandwich), with no (U.S.) mark.

states.label: American
states.question: Are the Hawaiian Islands American, in the colour of the United States?
states.cue: Labelled Hawaii (U.S.), Hawaiian Is. (U.S.) or Territory of Hawaii, in the same colour as the United States.

transitions.funFact: American planters and businessmen overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani in January 1893, backed by sailors and marines landed from a US warship, but President Cleveland refused to annex the islands. Their Republic of Hawaii waited until the war with Spain made the islands a useful stop on the way to the Philippines. The Hawaiian flag came down at ʻIolani Palace on 12 August 1898.

features.title: Saigon or Ho Chi Minh City
features.subject: City on the Mekong delta

states.label: Saigon
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Saigon (Saïgon), capital of South Vietnam from 1954 to 1975.

states.label: Ho Chi Minh City
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Ho Chi Minh City, sometimes with (Saigon) in brackets.

transitions.funFact: Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City on 2 July 1976, the day Vietnam was formally reunified, after the revolutionary leader who had died in 1969. Locals never stopped calling it Saigon, and in 2025 Saigon became the official name of its central district again.

features.title: Hong Kong and Macau: European colonies or Chinese
features.subject: Pearl River mouth

states.label: Both European
states.question: Are Hong Kong and Macau both marked as European colonies, British and Portuguese?
states.claim: Hong Kong and Macau are colonies
states.cue: Hong Kong is British (often pink, 'Br.') and Macau Portuguese ('Port.').

states.label: Hong Kong Chinese, Macau Portuguese
states.question: Is Hong Kong marked as part of China while Macau is still Portuguese?
states.claim: Hong Kong is Chinese, Macau Portuguese
states.cue: From July 1997 to December 1999 Hong Kong is a Chinese special administrative region, while Macau is still Portuguese.

states.label: Both Chinese
states.question: Are Hong Kong and Macau both marked as part of China?
states.claim: Hong Kong and Macau are Chinese
states.cue: Both are Chinese special administrative regions, often marked '(China)' or in China's colour.

transitions.funFact: Britain's lease on Hong Kong's New Territories, signed in 1898, ran for 99 years, and without them the colony could not survive. At midnight on 30 June 1997, after 156 years, Prince Charles and the last governor sailed away and Hong Kong became a Chinese region under 'one country, two systems'.

Macau, a Portuguese trading post since 1557, was the first European colony in China and the last to go. Portugal handed it back on 20 December 1999, just before the year 2000, closing more than four centuries of European colonial rule on the Chinese coast.

features.title: Hungary's outline: the old kingdom, Trianon Hungary, or wartime Hungary
features.subject: Hungary

states.label: The old kingdom
states.question: Is Hungary the big kingdom of the whole Carpathian basin, with Slovakia, Transylvania and Croatia inside it?
states.cue: The eastern half of Austria-Hungary: from the Tatra to the Iron Gates and down to the Adriatic at Fiume, often in one colour with Austria but with its own border.

states.label: Trianon Hungary
states.question: Is Hungary a small country of the plain, without Slovakia, Transylvania or a coast?
states.cue: Hungary keeps about a third of its old land around Budapest and the Great Plain; Slovakia, Transylvania and Croatia belong to its neighbours.

states.label: Wartime Hungary
states.question: Has Hungary grown back over southern Slovakia and northern Transylvania?
states.cue: Hungary reaches north into Slovakia and Ruthenia to the Polish border and east deep into Transylvania, cutting Romania in a deep bite.

states.label: Trianon Hungary
states.question: Is Hungary a small country of the plain, without Slovakia, Transylvania or a coast?
states.cue: Back to the Trianon border, with three small villages handed to Czechoslovakia opposite Bratislava.

transitions.funFact: Signed in the Grand Trianon palace at Versailles on 4 June 1920, the treaty left Hungary with only 28% of its old kingdom's land. Slovakia, Transylvania and Croatia went to its neighbours, and about 3.3 million Hungarians found themselves outside the new borders. In Hungary 'Trianon' is still a byword for national tragedy.

Hitler and Mussolini redrew Hungary's borders in two 'Vienna Awards': southern Slovakia in November 1938 and northern Transylvania in August 1940. With Ruthenia taken in 1939 and parts of Yugoslavia in 1941, Hungary briefly won back about a third of what it had lost, at the price of joining Hitler's war.

The armistice of January 1945 sent Hungary back to its Trianon borders, and the 1947 Paris peace treaty confirmed them. It even took a little more: three Hungarian villages opposite Bratislava went to Czechoslovakia, to give its capital of Slovakia room for a bridgehead on the Danube's southern bank.

features.title: Location of British India's capital: Calcutta or Delhi
features.subject: India's capital

states.label: Calcutta
states.question: Is the capital star at Calcutta, on the Bengal delta?
states.cue: The star of British India sits at Calcutta (Kalkutta), near the Bay of Bengal; Delhi is an ordinary city dot.

states.label: Delhi
states.question: Is the capital star at Delhi, with no New Delhi yet?
states.cue: The star sits at Delhi on the Jumna, far inland; New Delhi, then a building site south of the old city, is not printed yet. Calcutta is an ordinary city.

states.label: New Delhi
states.question: Is the capital star at New Delhi, in the north?
states.cue: The star is labelled New Delhi, the planned city just south of old Delhi; Calcutta is an ordinary city.

transitions.funFact: At the Delhi Durbar on 12 December 1911 King George V himself announced that India's capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi, the old Mughal capital. The decision had been kept so secret that the audience was stunned. Edwin Lutyens then built New Delhi beside the old city; it took twenty years.

New Delhi took almost twenty years to build. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker laid out its avenues, the Viceroy's House and the Secretariat on Raisina Hill, and the city was inaugurated in February 1931, just sixteen years before the British left India.

features.title: The East Indies: Dutch East Indies, United States of Indonesia, or Indonesia
features.subject: Islands between Asia and Australia

states.label: Dutch East Indies
states.question: Is the country of the East Indies called {name}?
states.cue: Labelled Dutch East Indies, Netherlands (East) Indies, or (Neth.).

states.label: United States of Indonesia
states.question: Is the country of the East Indies called {name}?
states.cue: Labelled United States of Indonesia (U.S.I.), a federation of sixteen states.

ja: インドネシア連邦共和国
インドネシア連邦共和国

states.label: Indonesia
states.question: Is the country of the East Indies called {name}?
states.cue: Labelled Indonesia (Republic of Indonesia).

transitions.funFact: When the Netherlands finally handed over sovereignty on 27 December 1949, it was to a federation of sixteen states, the United States of Indonesia, a design the Dutch favoured to dilute the revolutionary Republic. Western New Guinea stayed Dutch for thirteen more years.

The federation lasted less than eight months. One by one its member states voted to merge into the Republic, and on 17 August 1950, the fifth anniversary of the declaration of independence, Sukarno proclaimed a single unitary Republic of Indonesia.

features.title: Persia or Iran
features.subject: Country between Iraq and Afghanistan

states.label: Persia
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Persia (Perzië, Persien, Perse), the name used abroad for centuries.

states.label: Iran
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Iran, the country's own name, asked of foreigners from 1935; English maps of the 1940s-50s may still print Persia or Iran (Persia).

transitions.funFact: Reza Shah asked foreign governments to say Iran, the country's own name, from Nowruz 1935. During the war Churchill asked for Persia again to avoid confusion with Iraq, and in 1959 Iran agreed that both names could be used. Atlases took years to follow.

features.title: Ireland, Irish Free State, Eire, or Ireland
features.subject: Island west of Britain

states.label: Ireland (in the UK)
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Just Ireland: the whole island is part of the United Kingdom.

states.label: Irish Free State
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Irish Free State (Irischer Freistaat, État libre d'Irlande), a British dominion. Maps of 1922 to 1937.

states.label: Eire
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Eire (Éire), the name of the 1937 constitution, used especially on British maps from 1938 to the 1950s.

states.label: Ireland
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Ireland, Republic of Ireland or Irish Republic, since 1949.

transitions.funFact: After the War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty, 26 of Ireland's 32 counties became the Irish Free State on 6 December 1922, a self-governing dominion like Canada. The six north-eastern counties stayed in the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland.

De Valera's constitution of 29 December 1937 declared that the state's name is Éire, or in English Ireland. Britain chose to call it Eire, even in its laws, and declared that the new name gave Dublin no right to Northern Ireland.

The Republic of Ireland Act took effect on Easter Monday, 18 April 1949. It made Republic of Ireland the state's description, not its name; British maps and officials kept saying Eire for decades, and the word only left UK law in 1981.

features.title: A border across Ireland: one island in the UK, or Northern Ireland split off
features.subject: Ireland

states.label: No border
states.question: Is the whole island of Ireland part of the United Kingdom, with no border across it?
states.claim: All of Ireland is in the UK
states.cue: Ireland in the same colour as Great Britain, with no line cutting off the north-east.

states.label: Border, Northern Ireland in the UK
states.question: Is there a border across Ireland, with Northern Ireland part of the United Kingdom?
states.cue: A border runs from Lough Foyle to Carlingford Lough: the south is its own country (Irish Free State, later Eire or Ireland), the north-east stays British.

transitions.funFact: The border was meant to be provisional: a Boundary Commission was to adjust it to local wishes. When a newspaper leaked in November 1925 that it would move only small strips, both governments buried the report, which stayed unpublished until 1969, and the old county line of 1921 became the border that is still there.

features.title: Palestine, Israel's 1949 lines, with Sinai, or without
features.subject: Israel

states.label: Palestine, no Israel
states.question: Is the area labelled Palestine, with no Israel?
states.cue: Before 1948 the land between Egypt and Transjordan is the British mandate of Palestine, often in Britain's colour.

states.label: Narrow Israel
states.question: Does Israel have its narrow shape, without the Sinai?
states.cue: Israel is narrow in the middle, about 15 km wide near Netanya. The Sinai is Egyptian; before 1967 the West Bank belongs to Jordan and the Gaza Strip is run by Egypt.

states.label: Israel holds the Sinai
states.question: Does Israel hold the whole Sinai Peninsula, up to the Suez Canal?
states.cue: Israel's colour, or hatching marked "Israeli occupied", covers the Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank and the Golan Heights, with the ceasefire line along the Suez Canal.

states.label: Sinai back in Egypt
states.question: Does Israel have its narrow shape, without the Sinai?
states.cue: The Sinai is Egyptian again. The West Bank, Gaza and the Golan are usually drawn with dashed lines or hatching as occupied territories.

transitions.funFact: Britain's mandate ended at midnight on 14 May 1948 and David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel that afternoon. Arab armies invaded; the armistice lines of 1949, the Green Line, became Israel's de facto borders, with Jordan holding the West Bank and Egypt the Gaza Strip.

In six days of June 1967 Israel took the Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria, more than tripling the area it controlled. The Suez Canal became the front line and stayed closed for eight years.

At Camp David in 1978 Egypt's Sadat and Israel's Begin agreed to trade land for peace, and the 1979 treaty returned the Sinai in stages. The settlement of Yamit was evacuated and demolished before the final handover on 25 April 1982. Sadat had been assassinated six months earlier.

features.title: Constantinople or Istanbul
features.subject: City on the Bosporus

states.label: Constantinople
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Constantinople (Konstantinopel, Costantinopoli), the city's name in the West for 1,600 years.

states.label: Istanbul
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Istanbul (Estambul, Stambuł, Стамбул), the Turkish name; early on often with (Constantinople) in brackets.

transitions.funFact: On 28 March 1930 the name Constantinople, used for 1,600 years, was officially replaced by İstanbul, and Turkey asked other countries to use Turkish names for its cities. The US State Department switched that May, but Constantinople stayed the common Western name well into the 1930s.

features.title: Istria and Trieste: Austrian, Italian, or Yugoslav
features.subject: Head of the Adriatic

states.label: Austria-Hungary
states.question: Are Trieste and Istria part of Austria-Hungary?
states.cue: The whole head of the Adriatic, Trieste, Istria and Fiume, is in Austria-Hungary's colour; Italy ends west of Gorizia.

ja: オーストリア＝ハンガリー

states.label: Italian
states.question: Is all of Istria part of Italy, as far as Fiume?
states.cue: Italy's colour covers Istria, Fiume (Rijeka) and the hills behind Trieste up to the Julian Alps; Yugoslavia starts just east of Fiume.

states.label: Yugoslav
states.question: Is Istria part of Yugoslavia, with Italy ending at Trieste?
states.cue: Istria and Rijeka (Fiume) are Yugoslav; Italy keeps only a thin coastal strip around Trieste (a Free Territory on maps of 1947-54).

states.label: Croatian and Slovenian
states.question: Is Istria split between Croatia and Slovenia?
states.cue: Most of the peninsula and Rijeka are in Croatia; the north-western corner around Koper is Slovenia's short coast; Trieste stays Italian.

transitions.funFact: Italy entered the First World War partly to win Austria's Adriatic lands. The 1920 Treaty of Rapallo gave it Trieste, Istria, Zara and several islands, while Fiume became a free state, after the poet D'Annunzio had seized it for over a year, until Italy annexed it in 1924.

The 1947 peace treaty gave most of Istria and Fiume to Yugoslavia, and between 200,000 and 350,000 Italians left the region over the following years. Trieste itself became a Free Territory under the UN, run by Allied and Yugoslav troops, until it was split in 1954, with the city going to Italy.

When Yugoslavia broke up, Istria was split along the old border between the Croatian and Slovenian republics: Croatia took most of the peninsula, and Slovenia kept the corner around Koper, its only stretch of sea coast, less than 50 km long.

features.title: Itaipú reservoir and the drowned Guaíra Falls
features.subject: Paraná river, Brazil–Paraguay border

states.label: River and falls
states.question: Is the Paraná a river here, with the Guaíra Falls (Sete Quedas)?
states.claim: The Paraná has the Guaíra Falls
states.cue: A thin river along the border with a waterfall mark at Guaíra, labelled Sete Quedas or Salto de Guaíra.

ja: フォス・ド・イグアス

states.label: Itaipú lake
states.question: Is there a long lake on the border river, behind the Itaipú dam?
states.claim: A long lake lies behind Itaipú
states.cue: A long, narrow lake about 170 km from the dam north of Foz do Iguaçu up to Guaíra, labelled Itaipú; no falls.

transitions.funFact: The Guaíra Falls, eighteen cataracts in seven groups, were among the most powerful waterfalls on Earth. When Brazil and Paraguay closed the Itaipú dam in October 1982, the lake rose 100 metres in two weeks and the falls disappeared; Brazil's great poet Drummond wrote them a farewell.

features.title: Smyrna or İzmir
features.subject: Port on the Aegean coast of Anatolia

states.label: Smyrna
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Smyrna (Smyrne, Smirne, Esmirna), the old Greek-derived name.

states.label: İzmir
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: İzmir (Izmir), the Turkish name used on maps after 1930.

transitions.funFact: Smyrna was one of the great cosmopolitan ports of the Mediterranean until the Turkish army entered it in September 1922 and a great fire destroyed the Greek and Armenian quarters. Since 1930 its only official name has been İzmir.

features.title: Batavia, Djakarta or Jakarta
features.subject: Capital on Java

states.label: Batavia
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Batavia, the Dutch colonial name.

states.label: Djakarta
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Djakarta, the spelling used from independence until 1972.

states.label: Jakarta
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Jakarta, after the 1972 spelling reform.

transitions.funFact: The Dutch East India Company founded Batavia in 1619 on the ruins of the port of Jayakarta, and named it after the Batavians, a Germanic tribe the Dutch saw as their ancestors. The Japanese occupiers revived the old name in 1942, and it stuck with independence.

In August 1972 Indonesia and Malaysia adopted a common spelling for their language. Dutch-style "dj" became "j" and "tj" became "c", so Djakarta became Jakarta. Maps in languages that write the city with a Y, Dż or C never had a "dj" to drop, so for them nothing changed.

features.title: Johannesburg: no city yet on the Witwatersrand, or the gold-rush city
features.subject: Transvaal

states.label: No Johannesburg
states.question: Is there no Johannesburg south of Pretoria?
states.cue: Pretoria is marked, but no city south of it on the Witwatersrand; at most a mining district or the word Witwatersrand.

states.label: Johannesburg
states.question: Is there a city called Johannesburg just south of Pretoria?
states.cue: Johannesburg (Joanesburgo, Йоханнесбург) about 55 km south of Pretoria, often printed as big as Pretoria or bigger.

transitions.funFact: Early in 1886 prospectors struck the main gold reef of the Witwatersrand, and the mining camp on the farm Randjeslaagte was named Johannesburg that October. Nobody knows which of several officials called Johannes it honours, because the records were lost. Ten years later more than 100,000 people lived there, making it one of the fastest-growing cities ever.

features.title: Transjordan or Jordan
features.subject: Kingdom east of the Jordan river

states.label: Transjordan
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Transjordan (Trans-Jordan, Transjordanien), "beyond the Jordan". Before 1921 the area has no name of its own.

states.label: Jordan
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Jordan (Jordanien, Jordanie), the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, which since 1950 also held the West Bank.

transitions.funFact: At independence in 1946 the kingdom already called itself the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in Arabic, but the English-speaking world kept saying Transjordan. Only in June 1949, after the war that left it holding the West Bank, did the government insist on Jordan in English too.

sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States 1949, vol. VI, doc. 714: editorial note (Office of the Historian)

features.title: Jubaland: Kenya reaching the Juba River, or ceded to Italian Somaliland
features.subject: Kenya and Somalia

states.label: Kenya to the Juba
states.question: Does Kenya (British East Africa) reach east to the Juba River, with Kismayu inside it?
states.cue: British East Africa's north-east corner runs to the Juba River and takes in Kismayu; Italian Somaliland begins on the far bank.

states.label: Kismayu Italian
states.question: Does Kenya end at a straight line west of the Juba, with Kismayu in Italian Somaliland?
states.cue: Kenya's eastern border runs as a long straight line well short of the Juba; the strip beyond it, with Kismayu (Chisimaio), is Italian.

transitions.funFact: In 1915 Britain and France promised Italy colonial rewards for joining the war. This was one: on 29 June 1925 the Union Jack came down at Kismayu, and about 91,000 km² of Kenya became the Italian colony of Oltre Giuba, 'beyond the Juba'. It lasted barely a year before merging into Italian Somaliland.

features.title: The Kakhovka Reservoir on the lower Dnieper
features.subject: Lower Dnieper

states.label: Just the river
states.question: Does the Dnieper flow as an ordinary river below Zaporizhzhia, with no big lake?
states.claim: The Dnieper is a plain river here
states.cue: Only the river's line, winding through the marshy Great Meadow, before 1956 and again since 2023.

states.label: A long lake
states.question: Is there a long, wide lake on the Dnieper between Zaporizhzhia and Nova Kakhovka?
states.claim: A long lake lies on the lower Dnieper
states.cue: A long blue reservoir fills the valley from Zaporizhzhia almost to Kherson.

states.label: Just the river
states.question: Does the Dnieper flow as an ordinary river below Zaporizhzhia, with no big lake?
states.claim: The Dnieper is a plain river here
states.cue: The reservoir has drained; the river runs through the old lake bed.

transitions.funFact: The Kakhovka dam, finished in 1956, turned the lower Dnieper into a reservoir about 240 km long and up to 23 km wide, the largest in Ukraine by volume. It drowned the Great Meadow, the old Cossack heartland, and fed canals that watered the dry south and Crimea.

In the early hours of 6 June 2023, while the area was under Russian occupation, the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. Within weeks the reservoir had poured out towards the Black Sea, flooding towns downstream. Young willow and poplar forests are now growing on the old lake bed.

features.title: Tver, Kalinin, or Tver again
features.subject: City on the upper Volga

states.label: Tver
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Tver (Twer), the city's medieval name.

states.label: Kalinin
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Kalinin (Kalinine), after the Soviet head of state Mikhail Kalinin.

states.label: Tver
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Tver again since July 1990.

transitions.funFact: In November 1931 Tver was renamed after Mikhail Kalinin, the Soviet head of state, who was born nearby and was still alive. Ten years later, in the war, Kalinin became the first major European city the Red Army took back from the Wehrmacht, in December 1941.
Tver dropped its Soviet name on 17 July 1990, ahead of Gorky (October 1990) and of Leningrad and Sverdlovsk, which changed back only after the failed Moscow coup of August 1991.

features.title: Königsberg or Kaliningrad
features.subject: Port on the Pregel

states.label: Königsberg
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Königsberg (Koningsbergen, Królewiec), capital of East Prussia.

states.label: Kaliningrad
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Kaliningrad (Kaliningrado), after Mikhail Kalinin; German maps often keep Königsberg.

transitions.funFact: Kant lived his whole life in Königsberg, and its seven bridges inspired Euler's famous puzzle that founded graph theory. Captured in April 1945, the ruined city was renamed in July 1946 after Mikhail Kalinin, who had just died. Polish authorities now recommend the old Polish name Królewiec.

features.title: Kamerun's two arms to the Congo and Ubangi rivers (Neukamerun)
features.subject: Cameroon

states.label: No arms
states.question: Does Cameroon end in a closed outline, with no arms reaching the Congo river?
states.claim: Cameroon has a closed, compact outline
states.cue: Kamerun's eastern and southern borders run across the forest well short of the Congo; French Congo (later French Equatorial Africa) wraps round it.

states.label: Two arms to the Congo
states.question: Does Kamerun send two long arms south-east to the Congo and Ubangi rivers?
states.claim: Kamerun has two arms to the Congo
states.cue: German Kamerun is much bigger: one arm reaches the Congo near the mouth of the Sangha, another the Ubangi, and a strip of northern Gabon wraps round Spanish Guinea.

states.label: No arms
states.question: Does Cameroon end in a closed outline, with no arms reaching the Congo river?
states.claim: Cameroon has a closed, compact outline
states.cue: French Cameroun and the British Cameroons together fill the old outline again; the arms are back in French Equatorial Africa.

transitions.funFact: To end the Agadir Crisis, Germany let France have Morocco and took a slice of French Congo in return, almost 300,000 km². 'Neukamerun' reached the Congo and Ubangi rivers in two thin arms, so 'Grand Kamerun' grew by more than half. Critics at home called the new land worthless, and Germany's colonial secretary resigned over the deal.

Allied troops conquered Kamerun by early 1916, and France simply folded the two arms back into French Equatorial Africa. The rest was split along a line the French diplomat Georges Picot drew in pencil on a map in London, the same Picot who drew up the Middle East with Mark Sykes that spring. France got four-fifths, Britain two strips along Nigeria.

features.title: Kara-Bogaz-Gol lagoon on the Caspian Sea
features.subject: East shore of the Caspian

states.label: A big lagoon
states.question: Is there a big lagoon full of water on the Caspian's east shore, joined by a narrow strait?
states.claim: The lagoon is full of water
states.cue: A round lagoon, the Kara-Bogaz-Gol, about 150 km across, fed by a fast current from the Caspian through a narrow strait.

states.label: A salt flat
states.question: Is the lagoon gone, shown as a dry salt flat or as land?
states.cue: The strait is dammed and the lagoon has dried to a white salt flat.

states.label: A big lagoon
states.question: Is there a big lagoon full of water on the Caspian's east shore, joined by a narrow strait?
states.claim: The lagoon is full of water
states.cue: The dam is gone and the lagoon has filled again.

transitions.funFact: Worried that the Caspian Sea was shrinking, Soviet planners blamed the Kara-Bogaz-Gol, where Caspian water poured in and evaporated in the desert heat. In 1980 they dammed the strait. By 1984 the lagoon, once the world's biggest natural salt works, had dried into a salt flat whose dust blew over the region.

The Caspian had in fact started to rise again in 1978, so the dam was solving the wrong problem. Newly independent Turkmenistan broke it open in 1992, and the lagoon refilled within a few years, a rare case of an environmental mistake undone.

features.title: Location of Kazakhstan's capital
features.subject: Kazakhstan's capital

states.label: Capital in the south-east
states.question: Is the capital in the far south-east, at Alma-Ata (Almaty)?
states.cue: The capital star is at Alma-Ata (Almaty since 1993), at the foot of the Tian Shan.

states.label: Capital in the north
states.question: Is the capital in the northern steppe, at Akmola (Astana)?
states.cue: The star is at Astana (called Akmola in 1997-98, Nur-Sultan 2019-22) on the Ishim river; Almaty is an ordinary city.

transitions.funFact: President Nazarbayev moved Kazakhstan's capital 1,000 km north on 10 December 1997, from Almaty, squeezed between mountains and earthquake faults near China, to Akmola in the windswept steppe, where winter nights reach -40 °C. Officials cited room to grow and earthquake risk; critics saw a move to anchor the Russian-speaking north.

features.title: Kiaochow (Tsingtao): Chinese, German or Japanese
features.subject: Coast of Shantung

states.label: Chinese
states.question: Is the bay plain Chinese coast?
states.cue: Nothing marks the bay; it is part of China's Shantung province.

states.label: German
states.question: Is the bay marked as German, Kiautschou (Ger.)?
states.cue: A small territory around the bay in Germany's colour, labelled Kiautschou or Kiaochow (Ger.), with Tsingtao.

states.label: Japanese
states.question: Is the bay marked as Japanese, Kiaochow (Jap.)?
states.cue: The territory around the bay is in Japan's colour or marked (Jap.).

states.label: Chinese
states.question: Is the bay plain Chinese coast?
states.cue: Nothing marks the bay; Tsingtao is a Chinese port.

transitions.funFact: Germany used the murder of two missionaries as a pretext to seize Jiaozhou Bay, then forced China into a 99-year lease in March 1898. Its port, Tsingtao, got German villas, a cathedral, and in 1903 a brewery whose Tsingtao beer is still sold around the world.

Japan, Britain's ally, besieged Tsingtao in the autumn of 1914, and the German garrison surrendered on 7 November. It was the only real battle of the First World War in East Asia, and Japan kept the territory when the fighting ended.

The Treaty of Versailles handed Germany's rights in Shantung to Japan, which set off China's May Fourth protests in 1919. After a deal struck at the Washington Conference, Japan returned the territory to China on 10 December 1922.

features.title: Léopoldville or Kinshasa
features.subject: Capital on the Congo River

states.label: Léopoldville
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Léopoldville (Leopoldstad in Dutch), named after King Leopold II.

states.label: Kinshasa
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Kinshasa, since 1966.

transitions.funFact: Henry Morton Stanley founded Léopoldville in 1881 and named it after his employer, King Leopold II of Belgium. On the sixth anniversary of independence in 1966 Mobutu renamed it Kinshasa, after a village on the site, and Stanley's statue was later removed from the hill above the river.

features.title: Vyatka or Kirov
features.subject: City on the Vyatka river

states.label: Vyatka
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Vyatka (Wjatka, Viatka), named after its river.

states.label: Kirov
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Kirov (Kirow), after the Bolshevik Sergei Kirov.

transitions.funFact: The Soviet party leader Sergei Kirov was assassinated on 1 December 1934, and within days Vyatka, called Khlynov until 1780, was renamed after him. Unlike most Soviet names, Kirov was never changed back, despite campaigns to restore Vyatka.

features.title: Name of the big city on the Ganges delta
features.subject: City on the Ganges delta

states.label: Calcutta
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: The British spelling Calcutta (Kalkutta, Calcuta), used for three centuries.

states.label: Kolkata
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Kolkata, the Bengali form, official in English since 2001. Several languages kept their old spelling.

transitions.funFact: On 1 January 2001 West Bengal changed the city's official English name from Calcutta to Kolkata, matching how Bengali speakers had always said it; the name probably comes from the village of Kalikata. Calcutta had been the capital of British India until 1911.

features.title: One Korea, the 38th parallel, or the DMZ
features.subject: Korea

states.label: One Korea
states.question: Is Korea one undivided territory?
states.cue: No border across the peninsula: one Korea, the Korean Empire until 1910, then a Japanese colony labelled Korea or Chōsen.

states.label: Straight line
states.question: Do the two Koreas meet along a straight east–west line?
states.claim: The Koreas meet along a straight line
states.cue: From 1945 to 1953 the border is the 38th parallel, a perfectly straight line across the peninsula just north of Seoul.

states.label: Slanting armistice line
states.question: Does the border between the Koreas slant across the peninsula?
states.cue: Since the 1953 armistice the line runs from just north of Seoul on the west coast to well north of the 38th parallel on the east coast, often drawn with a narrow demilitarised zone (DMZ).

transitions.funFact: Two young American officers, given about half an hour and a National Geographic map, picked the 38th parallel on 10 August 1945 as the line between Soviet and American occupation zones in Korea. The temporary line became a border when two Korean states were proclaimed in 1948.

The Korean War swept the front from the far south of the peninsula to the Chinese border and back. When the armistice was signed on 27 July 1953, the line froze where the armies stood: south of the 38th parallel in the west, well north of it in the east, with a 4 km wide demilitarised zone.

features.title: Korea: in Japan's colour, or not
features.subject: Korea

states.label: Not Japanese
states.question: Does Korea have a colour of its own, unlike Japan?
states.claim: Korea has a colour of its own
states.cue: Korea (the Korean Empire before 1905; North and South Korea after 1945) is not in Japan's colour and carries no Japanese mark.

states.label: Japanese protectorate
states.question: Is Korea marked Japanese (Jap.), yet drawn on its own?
states.cue: Korea keeps its own outline, often its own colour, but its name carries (Jap.) or "Jap. Prot."; it is not yet in Japan's colour.

states.label: In Japan's colour
states.question: Is Korea in Japan's colour?
states.cue: The whole peninsula shares Japan's colour, labelled Chōsen, Korea (Jap.) or 朝鮮.

states.label: Not Japanese
states.question: Does Korea have a colour of its own, unlike Japan?
states.claim: Korea has a colour of its own
states.cue: Korea is not in Japan's colour; since 1945 there are two Koreas.

transitions.funFact: Victory over Russia in 1905 left Japan free to take Korea. In November Japanese troops surrounded the palace while ministers signed away Korea's foreign affairs; the emperor refused to sign. Maps began adding "(Jap.)" to Korea, five years before it was annexed outright.

Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it outright on 29 August 1910, renaming it Chōsen. For 35 years most world maps coloured the peninsula like Japan, which then stretched from Sakhalin to Taiwan.

Japan's surrender on 15 August 1945 ended colonial rule in Korea, a day still celebrated in both Koreas. Liberation did not bring one Korean state: Soviet and American troops split the peninsula at the 38th parallel within weeks.

features.title: Kosovo: Ottoman, Serbian or its own country
features.subject: Kosovo

states.label: Ottoman
states.question: Is Kosovo part of the Ottoman Empire, which still stretches across the Balkans?
states.cue: Before the Balkan Wars of 1912-13 the Ottoman Empire (often printed 'Turkey') reached from Constantinople to the Adriatic, and Kosovo lay deep inside it.

states.label: Part of Serbia or Yugoslavia
states.question: Is Kosovo part of Serbia or Yugoslavia, without a country border of its own?
states.cue: From 1913 Kosovo belongs to Serbia, and from 1918 to Yugoslavia. Maps show at most the thin boundary of the autonomous province.

states.label: Part of Serbia or Yugoslavia
states.question: Is Kosovo part of Serbia or Yugoslavia, without a country border of its own?
states.cue: Since Montenegro left in 2006, Kosovo lies inside a smaller Serbia; maps show at most the thin boundary of the province.

states.label: Its own country
states.question: Is Kosovo drawn as a country, with its own border and name?
states.cue: Since 2008 most maps draw Kosovo as a country; some use a dashed border or add a note that Serbia does not recognise it.

transitions.funFact: In the First Balkan War of 1912, Serbian and Montenegrin armies drove the Ottomans out of Kosovo within weeks. The Treaty of London in May 1913 confirmed that the Ottoman Empire had lost almost all of its European lands, which it had held for around 450 years.

Serbia and Montenegro, the last remnant of Yugoslavia, broke up after Montenegro's referendum passed in May 2006 with 55.5 percent, just over the 55 percent the EU had set. Kosovo stayed inside the smaller Serbia for twenty more months, until it declared independence itself.

Kosovo declared independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008, nine years after NATO's bombing campaign ended Serbian rule there. Around a hundred countries recognise it, but Serbia, Russia, China and five EU members do not, so some maps still draw Kosovo with a dashed border.

features.title: Samara, Kuybyshev, or Samara again
features.subject: City at the great bend of the Volga

states.label: Samara
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Samara, the city's old name.

states.label: Kuybyshev
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Kuybyshev (Kuibyschew, Kouïbychev), after the Bolshevik Valerian Kuybyshev.

states.label: Samara
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Samara again since January 1991.

transitions.funFact: Samara was renamed in January 1935 after the Bolshevik leader Valerian Kuybyshev. In October 1941, with the Germans near Moscow, the government was evacuated here: Kuybyshev became the Soviet Union's reserve capital, with a deep bunker built for Stalin that he never used.

On 25 January 1991, months before the Soviet Union ended, the city took back the name Samara after 56 years. Its wartime past survives underground: the bunker built for Stalin in case Moscow fell, which he never used.

features.title: Spelling of Ukraine's capital
features.subject: Big city on the Dnieper

states.label: Kiev
states.question: Is the city spelled {name}?
states.cue: The spelling taken from Russian: Kiev, Kiew, Kijów, キエフ.

states.label: Kyiv in English
states.question: Is the city spelled {name}?
states.cue: English maps switch to Kyiv, transliterated from Ukrainian, from mid-2019.

states.label: Kyiv in Japanese, Dutch and Danish
states.question: Is the city spelled {name}?
states.cue: From 2022 Japanese maps write キーウ, and Dutch and Danish ones Kyiv.

states.label: Kyjiw in German
states.question: Is the city spelled {name}?
states.cue: From 2024 German maps begin to write Kyjiw instead of Kiew.

transitions.funFact: Ukraine made Kyiv, transliterated from Ukrainian, the official Latin spelling in 1995, but the world kept writing Kiev, based on Russian. After the #KyivNotKiev campaign the US Board on Geographic Names switched in June 2019, and airports, newspapers and English-language atlases followed.

After Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 the spelling became a statement. Japan's foreign ministry dropped キエフ, based on Russian, for キーウ on 31 March 2022, and the Dutch government and broadcasters moved from Kiev to Kyiv over the following year.

Germany held out the longest of Ukraine's big partners. Its Foreign Office replaced Kiew with the Ukrainian-based Kyjiw on 24 February 2024, the second anniversary of the invasion, and Der Spiegel and Die Zeit followed in October 2024. Many German atlases still print Kiew.

features.title: Lado Enclave: does the Congo reach the Nile?
features.subject: Upper Nile

states.label: Congo short of the Nile
states.question: Does the Congo stop short of the Nile, along the watershed west of the river?
states.claim: The Congo stops short of the Nile
states.cue: The Congo's north-eastern border follows the Nile-Congo watershed, so Lado and the Upper Nile lie outside it, in the Sudan.

states.label: Congo on the Nile
states.question: Does the Congo reach the Nile, with a wedge of land around Lado on the river's west bank?
states.claim: The Congo reaches the Nile at Lado
states.cue: A wedge of the Congo Free State, the Lado Enclave, touches the White Nile north of Lake Albert, labelled Lado or "leased to the Congo State".

states.label: Congo short of the Nile
states.question: Does the Congo stop short of the Nile, along the watershed west of the river?
states.claim: The Congo stops short of the Nile
states.cue: The Congo's north-eastern border follows the Nile-Congo watershed, so Lado and the Upper Nile lie outside it, in the Sudan.

transitions.funFact: King Leopold II wanted a foothold on the Nile. In 1894 Britain leased him the river's west bank around Lado for the rest of his life, keeping France away from the Upper Nile. His Congo Free State troops only got there in February 1897, beating a Mahdist force at Rejaf, and the remote enclave became known for its elephants.

The lease ran only for Leopold's lifetime. He died in December 1909, and on 10 June 1910 the enclave passed to the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. In the months between, with nobody really in charge, ivory hunters poured in and shot almost all of an estimated 2,000 elephants before Sudanese officials took control.

features.title: Lake Albert or Lake Mobutu Sese Seko
features.subject: Lake on the Uganda–Congo border

states.label: Lake Albert
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Albert (Albertsee, Lac Albert).

states.label: Lake Mobutu Sese Seko
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Mobutu Sese Seko, often with (L. Albert) in brackets.

ja: モブツ・セセ・セコ湖
モブツ・セセ・セコ湖

states.label: Lake Albert
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Albert again.

transitions.funFact: Zaire's dictator Mobutu Sese Seko renamed many places in his "authenticity" campaign, and Lake Albert, named by the explorer Samuel Baker after Queen Victoria's husband, became Lake Mobutu Sese Seko. Atlases of the 1970s and 1980s often printed both names, one in brackets.

When Mobutu fled Kinshasa in May 1997, his name disappeared from the map along with Zaire itself, and the lake became Lake Albert again. Uganda, which holds the eastern half of the lake, had generally kept using the old name all along.

features.title: Lake Edward or Lake Idi Amin Dada
features.subject: Lake on the Uganda–Congo border

states.label: Lake Edward
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Edward (Eduardsee, Lac Édouard).

states.label: Lake Idi Amin Dada
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Idi Amin Dada, after Uganda's dictator.

ja: イディ・アミン・ダダ湖
イディ・アミン・ダダ湖

states.label: Lake Edward
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Edward again.

transitions.funFact: Henry Morton Stanley named the lake in 1888 after Queen Victoria's eldest son, the future Edward VII. In 1973 Uganda renamed it Lake Idi Amin Dada, after the country's dictator, and Zaire, which shares the lake, went along with it.

When Tanzanian troops and Ugandan exiles drove Idi Amin out in April 1979, his lake went back to being Lake Edward. Few foreign atlases had adopted the dictator's name, so a map that prints it is a rare and very precise clue.

features.title: Lake Kariba on the Zambezi
features.subject: Middle Zambezi

states.label: Just the river
states.question: Does the Zambezi run below the Victoria Falls as a plain river, with no long lake?
states.claim: The Zambezi is a plain river here
states.cue: Downstream of the Victoria Falls only the river's line marks the border.

states.label: Lake Kariba
states.question: Is there a long lake on the Zambezi, along the border below the Victoria Falls?
states.claim: A long lake lies on the Zambezi
states.cue: Lake Kariba stretches for about 220 km along the border, from the Victoria Falls region to the dam at Kariba.

transitions.funFact: The Kariba Dam, built from 1955 to 1959, created the world's largest reservoir by volume. As the water rose, Operation Noah rescued more than 6,000 animals stranded on shrinking islands, and some 57,000 Tonga people were moved off their land. They say their river god, Nyaminyami, was cut off from his wife.

features.title: Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam
features.subject: Nile in Nubia

states.label: Just the river
states.question: Does the Nile run south of Aswan as a narrow river, with no long lake?
states.claim: The Nile is a narrow river past Aswan
states.cue: South of Aswan only the Nile's thin line winds into Sudan past Wadi Halfa.

states.label: Lake Nasser
states.question: Is there a long lake on the Nile above Aswan, reaching into Sudan?
states.claim: A long lake lies above Aswan
states.cue: Lake Nasser fills the Nile valley from the Aswan High Dam into Sudan, where its southern end is called Lake Nubia.

transitions.funFact: To build the Aswan High Dam, Egypt flooded 500 km of the Nile valley, and UNESCO led a race to save the temples of Nubia. Abu Simbel's colossal statues were cut into blocks and rebuilt 65 metres higher. The old Sudanese town of Wadi Halfa disappeared under the water.

features.title: Lake Rudolf or Lake Turkana
features.subject: Long lake in northern Kenya

states.label: Lake Rudolf

states.cue: Lake Rudolf (Rudolfsee, Lac Rodolphe).

states.label: Lake Turkana
states.question: Is the lake called {name}?
states.cue: Lake Turkana (Turkanasee, Lac Turkana).

transitions.funFact: Count Teleki's Hungarian-Austrian expedition named the lake after Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria in 1888. Kenya renamed it Lake Turkana in 1975, after the people living on its shores. Russian and Polish maps still say Rudolf, so this clue only works in some languages.

features.title: Lake Volta in Ghana
features.subject: Central Ghana

states.label: Just rivers
states.question: Does the Volta cross central Ghana as an ordinary river, with no big lake?
states.claim: The Volta is an ordinary river
states.cue: Only the thin lines of the White and Black Volta, joining and running south to the sea east of Accra.

states.label: Lake Volta
states.question: Is there a huge branching lake in the middle of Ghana?
states.claim: A huge lake lies in the middle of Ghana
states.cue: Lake Volta, a long, branching blue lake behind the Akosombo Dam north-east of Accra, covering a large part of the country.

transitions.funFact: Ghana's Akosombo Dam, built to power an aluminium smelter, backed the Volta up into the largest artificial lake on Earth by area, covering 3.6 per cent of the country. About 78,000 people from 740 villages had to be resettled, and drowned forests still stand in the water.

features.title: Larsen A and B ice shelves on the Antarctic Peninsula
features.subject: Antarctic Peninsula

states.label: Ice to about 64° S
states.question: Does a shelf of floating ice line the peninsula's east coast north of 65° S?
states.claim: Ice lines the coast north of 65° S
states.cue: Larsen A and Larsen B form a continuous white fringe along the east coast up to about 64° S.

states.label: Ice from about 65° S
states.question: Does the ice shelf start around 65° S, with open water north of it?
states.claim: The ice shelf starts around 65° S
states.cue: Larsen A is gone; the white fringe begins at Larsen B, around 65° S.

states.label: Ice only south of 66° S
states.question: Is the coast open water as far south as 66° S, with the ice starting further south?
states.claim: The coast is open water to 66° S
states.cue: Larsen A and B are gone; only Larsen C remains, south of about 66° S.

transitions.funFact: In late January 1995 the Larsen A ice shelf, a slab of floating ice of roughly 1,500 to 2,300 square kilometres, broke up within days during a warm summer storm. Scientists had watched it shrink for decades, but the speed of the final break-up surprised them.

Between 31 January and March 2002 satellites watched 3,250 square kilometres of the Larsen B ice shelf, an area bigger than Luxembourg and about 220 metres thick, shatter into thousands of icebergs. Sediment cores suggest it had been stable for about 10,000 years, since the end of the last ice age.

features.title: Basutoland or Lesotho

states.label: Lesotho

states.cue: Independent Lesotho.

transitions.funFact: Basutoland, a mountain kingdom completely surrounded by South Africa, became independent as Lesotho on 4 October 1966. Its lowest point, about 1,400 metres above sea level, is the highest low point of any country, which is why it calls itself the Kingdom in the Sky.

features.title: Libya: Ottoman, Italian, under Allied rule, or independent
features.subject: Libya

states.label: Ottoman
states.question: Is Libya part of the Ottoman Empire?
states.cue: Before 1912 the coast around Tripoli and Benghazi belongs to the Ottoman Empire (Turkey), labelled Tripoli or Tripolitania, and Barca or Cyrenaica.

states.label: Italian colony
states.question: Is Libya an Italian colony?
states.cue: Painted in Italy's colour and labelled Libia, Libya (It.), or Tripolitania and Cyrenaica (It.).

states.label: British and French zones
states.question: Is Libya split into British- and French-run zones?
states.claim: Libya is in British and French zones
states.cue: No longer Italian: Tripolitania and Cyrenaica under British military administration, the Fezzan in the south-west under French. Maps print the three names, often with (Br.) or (Fr.).

states.label: Independent
states.question: Is Libya an independent country?
states.cue: One country, Libya, in its own colour: a kingdom from 1951, a republic after 1969.

transitions.funFact: Italy invaded the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica in 1911, in the first war in which bombs were dropped from aeroplanes. Under the Treaty of Ouchy of 18 October 1912 the Ottomans withdrew. Italy revived the Roman name Libya, but needed twenty more years of brutal fighting to control the interior.

The British Eighth Army took Tripoli on 23 January 1943 and pushed the last Axis troops out of Libya weeks later. Britain then ran Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, and Free French forces held the Fezzan. Italy formally gave up the colony in the 1947 peace treaty.

Libya was the first country to win independence through a decision of the United Nations, on 24 December 1951, as a kingdom under Idris, head of the Senussi order. It was then one of the poorest countries on earth; oil was found in 1959 and changed everything.

states.claim: Madagascar has a colour of its own
states.cue: The island in its own colour, labelled Madagascar or Malagasy Republic (République malgache), with no (Fr.) mark.

transitions.funFact: France claimed Madagascar as a protectorate after a war in 1883-85, but the Merina court read the 1885 treaty differently, and Britain had missionaries and traders on the island. The deadlock broke on 5 August 1890, when Britain recognised the French protectorate in return for France accepting Britain's over Zanzibar, one of that summer's swaps of African land between European capitals.

A French expedition landed in 1895 and took Antananarivo on 30 September, though far more of its soldiers died of disease than in battle. After a revolt, a law of 6 August 1896 made the island a French colony, and General Gallieni sent Queen Ranavalona III into exile in February 1897, ending the Merina monarchy.

Madagascar became an autonomous Malagasy Republic within the French Community in October 1958 and fully independent on 26 June 1960, with Philibert Tsiranana as president. Its early years stayed close to France, but colonial rule had left a deep scar: the French army had crushed the 1947 uprising at a cost of tens of thousands of lives.

features.title: British Central Africa, Nyasaland or Malawi
features.subject: West of Lake Nyasa

states.label: British Central Africa
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: The British Central Africa Protectorate (B.C.A.).
