transitions.funFact: Canada and Newfoundland argued for decades over how far inland Labrador went. On 1 March 1927 the Privy Council in London ruled for Newfoundland, setting the border on the watershed far inland. Quebec has never officially accepted the line.

In 1933 Newfoundland's parliament voted itself out of existence and handed power to a British-appointed commission. In a second referendum in July 1948, 52.3 percent voted to join Canada, and at midnight on 31 March 1949 it became the tenth province, the last to join.

features.title: The Niger delta: Oil Rivers, Niger Coast, Southern Nigeria or Nigeria
features.subject: Coast of the Niger delta

states.label: Oil Rivers Protectorate
states.question: Is the land on the Niger delta called {name}?
states.cue: The coast of the delta is labelled Oil Rivers (Protectorate), after the palm oil traded there.

states.label: Niger Coast Protectorate
states.question: Is the land on the Niger delta called {name}?
states.cue: The delta coast is labelled Niger Coast Protectorate; the Royal Niger Company holds the land up the river.

states.label: Southern Nigeria
states.question: Is the land on the Niger delta called {name}?
states.cue: The south is labelled Southern Nigeria, with Northern Nigeria inland.

states.label: Nigeria
states.question: Is the land on the Niger delta called {name}?
states.cue: One name, Nigeria, covers the delta and the land far inland.

transitions.funFact: The Oil Rivers were named for palm oil, not petroleum: the delta's creeks carried palm oil to British traders for soap, candles and machine grease. In May 1893 the protectorate was renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate and pushed inland.

On 1 January 1900 the Crown took over the Royal Niger Company's lands and joined the coastal part to the Niger Coast Protectorate as Southern Nigeria. The name Nigeria itself had been coined only in 1897, by the journalist Flora Shaw in The Times.

Frederick Lugard, Flora Shaw's husband, merged Northern and Southern Nigeria into one colony on 1 January 1914, largely so that the richer south could pay for the north. The amalgamation drew the outline of what is now Africa's most populous country.

features.title: Nigeria: Niger territories, Northern and Southern Nigeria, or one Nigeria
features.subject: Lower Niger

states.label: No Nigeria yet
states.question: Is there no Nigeria yet, only Lagos, the Niger Coast and the Niger company lands?
states.claim: The Niger Company holds the interior
states.cue: The coast is the Oil Rivers or Niger Coast Protectorate, Lagos a small colony, and the interior Royal Niger Company territory, or just Sokoto and Bornu; the name Nigeria is missing.

states.label: Northern and Southern Nigeria
states.question: Is the British land on the Niger split into Northern and Southern Nigeria?
states.claim: Northern and Southern Nigeria are split
states.cue: Two protectorates in Britain's colour, labelled Northern Nigeria and Southern Nigeria, with a border across the middle.

states.label: One Nigeria
states.question: Is Nigeria one territory, from the coast to Lake Chad?
states.cue: One label, Nigeria, across the whole territory, with no border between north and south.

transitions.funFact: On New Year's Day 1900 the British Crown took over the Royal Niger Company's lands and created the protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria. The name itself was new: the journalist Flora Shaw had suggested 'Nigeria', after the river, in The Times in January 1897.

Frederick Lugard, the soldier whose troops had conquered the north, merged Northern and Southern Nigeria into one colony on 1 January 1914 and became its first governor-general. By then he had married Flora Shaw, the journalist who had suggested the country's name seventeen years earlier.

features.title: Name of the city where the Oka meets the Volga
features.subject: City where the Oka meets the Volga

states.label: Nizhny Novgorod
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Nizhny Novgorod, 'Lower Newtown', before 1932 and again since 1990.

states.label: Gorky
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Gorky (Gorki, Горький), after the writer Maxim Gorky, 1932-1990.

states.label: Nizhny Novgorod
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Nizhny Novgorod again since October 1990.

transitions.funFact: In 1932, to celebrate forty years of Maxim Gorky's writing career, Stalin renamed the writer's home city after him, while Gorky was still alive. Moscow's main street, a park and a car factory took his name too, and in the city the cars were made: the GAZ Volga.

Gorky was a closed city, off limits to foreigners, which is why the Soviet government exiled the dissident physicist Andrei Sakharov there from 1980 to 1986. On 22 October 1990, as the Soviet Union opened up, it took back its 800-year-old name, Nizhny Novgorod.

features.title: Northern Territory, or North Australia and Central Australia
features.subject: Northern Australia

states.label: Northern Territory
states.question: Is it one territory, the Northern Territory, from Darwin to the South Australian border?
states.claim: The Northern Territory is one territory
states.cue: One Northern Territory between Western Australia and Queensland, with no line across it.

states.label: North and Central Australia
states.question: Is it split along the 20th parallel into North Australia and Central Australia?
states.claim: North and Central Australia are split
states.cue: A straight line at 20° S, with North Australia (capital Darwin) above it and Central Australia (capital Stuart, later Alice Springs) below.

states.label: Northern Territory
states.question: Is it one territory, the Northern Territory, from Darwin to the South Australian border?
states.claim: The Northern Territory is one territory
states.cue: The Northern Territory again, as one.

transitions.funFact: In 1927 the federal government cut the Northern Territory in two along the 20th parallel: North Australia, to be developed by a commission based in Darwin, and Central Australia, run from the little telegraph town of Stuart, today's Alice Springs. Worries that the empty north invited invasion were part of the reason.

The North Australia Commission cost about £27,500 a year, and once the Great Depression hit, critics called it an extravagance. On 11 June 1931, barely four years after the split, the two territories became the Northern Territory again, and the line along the 20th parallel vanished from the map.

features.title: Name of the country around Skopje
features.subject: Country around Skopje

states.label: Turkey (Ottoman Empire)
states.question: Is the country around Skopje called {name}?
states.cue: Before 1913 Skopje (Üsküb) is an Ottoman city; maps print Turkey or the Ottoman Empire across the region.

states.label: Yugoslavia
states.question: Is the country around Skopje called {name}?
states.cue: From 1913 Serbia, and from 1918 the South Slav kingdom, Yugoslavia: no country of its own around Skopje.

states.label: Macedonia
states.question: Is the country around Skopje called {name}?
states.cue: Macedonia, often with '(F.Y.R.O.M.)' or 'Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia' because of Greece's objections.

states.label: North Macedonia
states.question: Is the country around Skopje called {name}?
states.cue: North Macedonia, the name agreed with Greece in 2018 and official since February 2019.

transitions.funFact: The Treaty of Bucharest that ended the Second Balkan War in August 1913 split the region of Macedonia between Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria. Serbia got the north around Skopje, a city the Ottoman Empire had held since the 1390s.

In a referendum on 8 September 1991 Macedonia voted to leave Yugoslavia, the only republic to do so without a war. Greece objected to the name, which it sees as part of its own heritage, so the country joined the United Nations in 1993 as 'the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia'.

The Prespa agreement, named after the lake where the two countries meet, ended a 27-year naming dispute with Greece. On 12 February 2019 the country officially became North Macedonia, and Greece dropped its veto on NATO membership, which followed in March 2020.

features.title: Nunavut split from the Northwest Territories
features.subject: Canadian Arctic

states.label: One Northwest Territories
states.question: Is northern Canada one huge Northwest Territories, with no Nunavut?
states.cue: The Northwest Territories cover all of Canada's mainland north of 60° east of the Yukon, plus the Arctic islands.

states.label: Nunavut split off
states.question: Is the eastern Arctic a separate territory, Nunavut, with its own boundary?
states.cue: A boundary splits the old Northwest Territories: Nunavut in the east, around Hudson Bay and Baffin Island, with its capital Iqaluit.

transitions.funFact: After two decades of negotiation with the Inuit, Canada split the Northwest Territories on 1 April 1999 and created Nunavut, 'our land' in Inuktitut. It covers a fifth of Canada, more than Western Europe's biggest countries put together, with only about 25,000 people at the start, most of them Inuit.

features.title: Godthåb or Nuuk
features.subject: Capital of Greenland

states.label: Godthåb
states.question: Is the town called {name}?
states.cue: Godthåb (Godthaab), the Danish name.

states.label: Nuuk
states.question: Is the town called {name}?
states.cue: Nuuk, the Greenlandic name; Danish maps add (Godthåb) for years.

transitions.funFact: Godthåb, "Good Hope", was founded in 1728 by the Norwegian missionary Hans Egede. When Greenland got home rule on 1 May 1979, Greenlandic names became official and the capital became Nuuk, "the headland". Danish maps kept printing Godthåb in brackets for years.

features.title: Indian Territory, Oklahoma Territory, or the state of Oklahoma
features.subject: Between Kansas and Texas

states.label: Indian Territory
states.question: Is all the land between Kansas and Texas Indian Territory, with the panhandle left as a strip of its own?
states.claim: The land is all Indian Territory
states.cue: Indian Territory (Ind. Ter.) across the whole area, often with the lands of the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw and other nations named inside. The panhandle is a separate strip, unlabelled or called No Man's Land or Public Land.

states.label: Two territories
states.question: Are there two territories side by side, Oklahoma Territory in the west and Indian Territory in the east?
states.cue: Oklahoma Territory (Okla. Ter., O.T.) in the west, including the panhandle, and Indian Territory (Ind. Ter., I.T.) in the east, with a jagged line between them; capital Guthrie.

states.label: State of Oklahoma
states.question: Is it one state called Oklahoma, panhandle included, with no Indian Territory?
states.cue: One state, Oklahoma (Okla.), from the panhandle to Arkansas; no Indian Territory anywhere.

transitions.funFact: At noon on 22 April 1889 about 50,000 settlers raced into the Unassigned Lands, and Guthrie and Oklahoma City had some 10,000 people each by nightfall. A year later Congress made the area Oklahoma Territory and added the panhandle, a strip that had had no government at all since 1850 and was known as No Man's Land.

The Five Tribes wanted Indian Territory to become a state of its own, named Sequoyah after the Cherokee scholar who created a writing system for his language, but Congress refused in 1905. Instead both territories became one state in 1907. Its name comes from the Choctaw words okla, people, and humma, red, suggested by Choctaw chief Allen Wright.

features.title: Muscat and Oman or Oman
features.subject: South-east Arabia

states.label: Muscat and Oman
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Muscat and Oman (Maskat und Oman, Mascate et Oman).

ja: マスカット・オマーン
マスカット・オマーン

states.label: Oman
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Just Oman (Sultanate of Oman).

transitions.funFact: Sultan Said bin Taimur ran Muscat and Oman as a closed country with three schools, and even banned sunglasses. His son Qaboos deposed him on 23 July 1970 and, seventeen days later, dropped "Muscat" from the name to show that the coast and the interior were now one Sultanate of Oman.

features.title: Name of Norway's capital: Christiania (Kristiania) or Oslo
features.subject: Norway's capital

states.label: Christiania (Kristiania)
states.question: Is the capital called {name}?
states.cue: Named after the Danish king Christian IV, spelled Christiania or, from the late 1870s, Kristiania.

states.label: Oslo
states.question: Is the capital called {name}?
states.cue: The medieval name, brought back for the capital.

transitions.funFact: After a fire in 1624, King Christian IV rebuilt the city beside Akershus fortress and named it Christiania after himself. Twenty years after Norway left its union with Sweden, a Danish king's name felt wrong, and on 1 January 1925 the capital took back its medieval name, Oslo. The old district of Oslo had to become Gamlebyen, 'the old town'.

features.title: Micronesia: German and Spanish, Japanese, a US trust territory, or independent
features.subject: Islands of the western Pacific

states.label: German and Spanish
states.question: Are these islands German or Spanish colonies?
states.claim: The islands are German or Spanish
states.cue: Island groups marked (Ger.) or (Sp.): the Marshall Islands German, the Carolines and Marianas Spanish until 1899 and German after. Often printed as part of German New Guinea.

states.label: Japanese mandate
states.question: Are the islands in Japan's colour, as a Japanese mandate?
states.claim: The islands are a Japanese mandate
states.cue: The islands share Japan's colour or carry "(Jap. Mand.)", "Japanese Mandated Islands" or 南洋群島.

states.label: US trust territory
states.question: Are the islands labelled as one US trust territory?
states.claim: The islands are a US trust territory
states.cue: One long label across the ocean, "Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (U.S.)" or "U.S. Trust Terr.", grouping the Marianas, Carolines and Marshalls.

en: Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
fr: Territoire sous tutelle des îles du Pacifique
es: Territorio en Fideicomiso de las Islas del Pacífico
it: Territorio fiduciario delle Isole del Pacifico
ja: 太平洋諸島信託統治領

states.label: Separate countries
states.question: Are the islands split into the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Palau and the Northern Marianas?
states.claim: The islands are split into countries
states.cue: Separate names: Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Palau, and Northern Mariana Islands (U.S.).

transitions.funFact: Having lost Guam and the Philippines to the United States in 1898, Spain sold its remaining Pacific islands, the Carolines and Marianas, to Germany for 25 million pesetas. Germany kept them only fifteen years: Japan seized them in 1914 and ruled them as a League of Nations mandate.

After capturing the islands in 1944 the United States ran them as the only "strategic" UN trust territory, which allowed military use. From 1946 to 1958 it exploded 67 nuclear bombs at Bikini and Enewetak in the Marshalls, including the 15-megaton Castle Bravo.

sources.title: Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (Wikipedia)

transitions.funFact: The trust territory voted itself apart. The Marianas chose to become a US commonwealth, Palau and the Marshalls refused to join the rest, and in 1986 the Marshall Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia became sovereign states in "free association" with the US, which kept their defence.

sources.title: Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (Wikipedia)

features.title: British India, a two-part Pakistan, or Pakistan and Bangladesh
features.subject: Pakistan

states.label: British India
states.question: Is the whole subcontinent British India, with no Pakistan?
states.cue: Before 1947 one British colour covers everything from Karachi to the Burmese border, labelled India or British India, dotted with princely states.

states.label: Pakistan in two parts
states.question: Is Pakistan in two pieces, with India in between?
states.cue: Pakistan has a western part around the Indus and an eastern part in Bengal, East Pakistan, both in the same colour, about 1,600 km apart.

states.label: Pakistan and Bangladesh
states.question: Are Pakistan and Bangladesh two separate countries?
states.cue: The former East Pakistan is Bangladesh, in its own colour, with its capital at Dhaka (Dacca).

transitions.funFact: British India was partitioned at midnight on 14–15 August 1947. Muslim-majority areas in the north-west and in eastern Bengal became Pakistan, a country in two pieces 1,600 km apart. Around 15 million people crossed the new borders, and hundreds of thousands died in the violence.

East Pakistan had more people than the west but little power, and in 1970 its Awami League won the national election outright. The army's crackdown in March 1971 started a war; India joined in December, and on 16 December Pakistan's army surrendered in Dhaka. Bangladesh means "land of the Bengalis".

features.title: Location of Pakistan's capital
features.subject: Pakistan's capital

states.label: No Pakistan yet
states.question: Is there no Pakistan yet, only British India?
states.cue: Before 1947 Karachi is a port of British India and there is no Pakistan on the map.

states.label: Capital at Karachi
states.question: Is Karachi, on the coast, Pakistan's capital?
states.cue: The capital star sits at Karachi near the mouth of the Indus.

states.label: Capital at Rawalpindi
states.question: Is Rawalpindi, in the north, Pakistan's capital?
states.cue: The capital star has moved north to Rawalpindi while Islamabad is built next to it; some maps print "Rawalpindi (provisional capital)".

states.label: Capital at Islamabad
states.question: Is Islamabad Pakistan's capital?
states.cue: The capital star is at Islamabad, a planned city at the foot of the hills in the north, beside Rawalpindi.

transitions.funFact: When Pakistan was created in August 1947, Karachi, a port of about 400,000 people, became its capital almost by default. Within a few years refugees from India had swelled it past a million, and ministries worked out of barracks and tents.

General Ayub Khan, who seized power in 1958, wanted his capital away from Karachi's business interests and close to the army headquarters at Rawalpindi. In 1959 Rawalpindi became the provisional capital while a new city, Islamabad, was laid out next to it by the Greek planner Constantinos Doxiadis.

Islamabad, "city of Islam", took over as capital in 1967, built from scratch on a grid of sectors at the foot of the Margalla Hills. Rawalpindi lies only about 15 km away, so on a globe the capital barely moves; only the name beside the star changes.

features.title: Panama Canal and the US Canal Zone
features.subject: Panama Canal

states.label: No canal, no zone
states.question: Is there no canal across Panama?
states.claim: The Isthmus of Panama is uncut
states.cue: The isthmus has no canal and no special zone. Before 1903 Panama is even part of Colombia.

states.label: Zone, canal unfinished
states.question: Is the Panama Canal still being built?
states.claim: The Panama Canal is being built
states.cue: A US Canal Zone is marked across the isthmus, but the canal itself is dotted, dashed or labelled 'under construction'.

states.label: Canal inside a US zone
states.question: Is the canal inside a US Canal Zone?
states.claim: The canal is in a US Canal Zone
states.cue: A finished canal with a narrow strip on either side marked as American: Canal Zone, C.Z. or (U.S.).

states.label: Canal, no zone
states.question: Is there a canal but no Canal Zone?
states.cue: The canal is drawn, but there's no separate zone around it. Since 1979 it's all Panama.

transitions.funFact: After backing Panama's break from Colombia in November 1903, the United States obtained a strip about ten miles wide across the isthmus by treaty. American officials formally took over on 4 May 1904 and restarted the canal that a French company had abandoned in the 1880s.

The Panama Canal opened to shipping on 15 August 1914, just as the First World War broke out in Europe, which muted the celebrations. Ships sailing between the Atlantic and the Pacific no longer had to go all the way around South America.

Under the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, the Canal Zone was abolished on 1 October 1979 and Panama took over the territory overnight. The canal itself was run jointly until noon on 31 December 1999, when it passed fully to Panama.

features.title: Panama: a department of Colombia or an independent country
features.subject: Isthmus of Panama

states.label: Part of Colombia
states.question: Is the Isthmus of Panama part of Colombia, in Colombia's colour?
states.cue: Colombia's colour runs west across the isthmus to the Costa Rican border; Panama is only a department name inside it, at most behind a thin internal line.

states.label: Panama independent
states.question: Is Panama a country of its own, separate from Colombia?
states.claim: Panama is a country of its own
states.cue: A full border where the isthmus meets South America, with Panama in its own colour; often with the American Canal Zone across its middle.

transitions.funFact: After Colombia's senate rejected a US canal treaty, rebels in Panama, funded by the French engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla, declared independence on 3 November 1903 while the USS Nashville kept Colombian troops away. Washington recognised the republic within days, and Bunau-Varilla, now Panama's envoy, signed the canal treaty on 18 November without a single Panamanian signature.

features.title: German New Guinea, Australian New Guinea, or Papua New Guinea
features.subject: Eastern New Guinea

states.label: German north
states.question: Is the north-east of New Guinea German?
states.cue: The north-east (Kaiser-Wilhelmsland) and the Bismarck Archipelago are German; the south-east is British Papua, run by Australia.

ja: ドイツ領ニューギニア

states.label: Australian
states.question: Is eastern New Guinea run by Australia?
states.cue: Papua in the south and the former German north (New Guinea) share Australia's colour, marked (Austr.) or Territory of Papua and New Guinea.

states.label: Papua New Guinea
states.question: Is Papua New Guinea an independent country?
states.cue: Eastern New Guinea and its islands have their own colour, labelled Papua New Guinea (P.N.G.).

transitions.funFact: Weeks into the First World War, an Australian force landed near Rabaul and the German colony surrendered on 17 September 1914. Germany gave it up under the Treaty of Versailles, and in December 1920 the League of Nations made it an Australian mandate: Kaiser-Wilhelmsland became the Territory of New Guinea.

Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia on 16 September 1975. With more than 800 languages, about a tenth of all the languages on Earth, it is the most linguistically diverse country in the world. Its first prime minister, Michael Somare, held the job for about seventeen years in total.

features.title: Perm or Molotov
features.subject: City on the Kama

states.label: Perm
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Perm (Perm', Пермь).

states.label: Molotov
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Molotov (Molotow, Mołotow), after Stalin's foreign minister.

states.label: Perm
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Perm again, as before 1940.

transitions.funFact: Perm was renamed Molotov on 8 March 1940, the eve of the 50th birthday of Vyacheslav Molotov, Stalin's foreign minister. He had signed the pact with Nazi Germany the year before, and the Finns had already named the petrol bomb after him: the Molotov cocktail.

Molotov plotted against Khrushchev in 1957, lost, and was sent off to Mongolia as ambassador. Within months the city named after him became Perm again, on 2 October 1957, and the Molotov region became the Perm region.

features.title: The Philippines: Spanish, American, or independent
features.subject: Philippines

states.label: Spanish colony
states.question: Are the islands a Spanish colony?
states.cue: Labelled Islas Filipinas or Philippine Islands (Sp.), in Spain's colour.

ja: フィリピン（スペイン領）

states.label: American
states.question: Are the islands American, marked (U.S.)?
states.cue: Labelled Philippine Islands (U.S.) or Philippines (Am.), in the United States' colour. The Commonwealth of 1935-46 looks the same.

states.label: Independent
states.question: Are the Philippines an independent country?
states.cue: Plain Philippines or Republic of the Philippines, with its own colour and the capital Manila (Quezon City on some maps of 1948-76).

transitions.funFact: Filipino revolutionaries under Emilio Aguinaldo declared independence from Spain in June 1898, but neither Spain nor the United States accepted it. In the Treaty of Paris of December 1898 Spain ceded the islands to the Americans, who then fought a long war against the new republic.

The United States recognised Philippine independence on 4 July 1946, its own Independence Day, after a promise made in the 1930s and delayed by the Japanese occupation. The treaty signed in Manila that day ended almost half a century of American rule.

features.title: Portugal's Pink Map: a Portuguese belt across Africa from Angola to Mozambique
features.subject: South-central Africa

states.label: Belt across Africa
states.question: Does Portugal's colour run across Africa, joining Angola to Mozambique?
states.cue: One Portuguese colour (usually pink, hence the name) from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, across the lands that became Northern and Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.

ja: アンゴラ (ポルトガル領)
モザンビーク (ポルトガル領)

depictions.label: Belt across Africa
depictions.question: Does Portugal's colour run across Africa, joining Angola to Mozambique?
depictions.cue: One Portuguese colour (usually pink, hence the name) from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, across the lands that became Northern and Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.

depictions.label: Two separate colonies
depictions.question: Are Angola and Mozambique two separate colonies, with other land between them?
depictions.cue: Angola on the Atlantic and Mozambique on the Indian Ocean, with unclaimed or British territory between them.

ja: アンゴラ (ポルトガル領)
モザンビーク (ポルトガル領)

states.label: Two separate colonies
states.question: Are Angola and Mozambique two separate colonies, with other land between them?
states.cue: Angola on the Atlantic and Mozambique on the Indian Ocean, with British Central Africa and the Rhodesias between them.

ja: アンゴラ (ポルトガル領)
モザンビーク (ポルトガル領)

transitions.funFact: In the mid-1880s Portugal published a map painting a pink belt right across Africa, linking Angola to Mozambique. Britain, with Cecil Rhodes's company pushing north, sent an ultimatum on 11 January 1890, and Portugal backed down. The humiliation inspired a song, A Portuguesa, now the national anthem, whose chorus first called for a march against the Britons.

features.title: Poland: partitioned, interwar, wiped off the map, or shifted west
features.subject: Poland

states.label: No Poland (three empires)
states.question: Is there no Poland, with Warsaw inside the Russian Empire?
states.claim: Warsaw is in the Russian Empire
states.cue: Warsaw lies in Russia; Germany and Austria-Hungary hold the west and south. At most a province name like Congress Poland or Galicia.

ja: オーストリア＝ハンガリー

states.label: Interwar Poland
states.question: Does Poland reach far east, bordering Latvia and Romania?
states.cue: A large Poland with Wilno and Lwów in the east, a narrow corridor to the Baltic at Gdynia, and the Free City of Danzig beside it. East Prussia is cut off from Germany.

states.label: Wiped off the map (1939–45)
states.question: Is Poland split between Germany and the Soviet Union?
states.cue: No Poland: the west is part of Germany, the middle is the German General Government around Warsaw and Kraków, and the east is Soviet, along a line on the Bug and San rivers.

depictions.label: Split between Germany and the USSR
depictions.question: Is Poland split between Germany and the Soviet Union?
depictions.cue: No Poland: German colour in the west and the General Government, Soviet colour east of the Bug.

depictions.label: Pre-war Poland, marked occupied
depictions.question: Does Poland reach far east, bordering Latvia and Romania?
depictions.cue: Allied maps often kept the 1939 borders, sometimes with a note such as "German occupied" or "Soviet occupied".

states.label: Shifted west
states.question: Does Poland reach west to the Oder and Neisse rivers?
states.claim: Poland reaches the Oder and Neisse
states.cue: Poland has moved west: Stettin (Szczecin), Breslau (Wrocław) and Danzig (Gdańsk) are Polish, the east ends at the Bug, and the long Baltic coast runs to the Oder.

depictions.label: Oder-Neisse border
depictions.question: Does Poland reach west to the Oder and Neisse rivers?
depictions.claim: Poland reaches the Oder and Neisse
depictions.cue: Poland has moved west: Stettin (Szczecin), Breslau (Wrocław) and Danzig (Gdańsk) are Polish, the east ends at the Bug, and the long Baltic coast runs to the Oder.

depictions.label: Germany's 1937 border still drawn
depictions.question: Is Germany's old 1937 border still drawn, dashed, around western Poland and East Prussia?
depictions.cue: West German maps and school atlases marked the 1937 border round Silesia, Pomerania and East Prussia, as lands only placed under Polish or Soviet administration until a peace treaty.

states.label: Post-war Poland
states.question: Does Poland reach west to the Oder and Neisse rivers?
states.claim: Poland reaches the Oder and Neisse
states.cue: Poland has moved west: Stettin (Szczecin), Breslau (Wrocław) and Danzig (Gdańsk) are Polish, the east ends at the Bug, and the long Baltic coast runs to the Oder.

transitions.funFact: After 123 years of partition between Russia, Prussia and Austria, Poland reappeared at the end of the First World War. Its eastern border was fought for until the Peace of Riga in March 1921, which set it some 250 km east of the line the Allies had proposed.

Germany invaded on 1 September 1939 and the Soviet Union on 17 September. On 28 September the two powers signed a treaty dividing Poland along the Bug and San rivers, swapping a slice of central Poland for Soviet control of Lithuania.

Poland came out of the war about 250 km further west. It lost 45 percent of its pre-war land to the Soviet Union and gained German Silesia, Pomerania and part of East Prussia. Millions of Poles and Germans were moved to fit the new borders.

sources.title: Territorial changes of Poland immediately after World War II (Wikipedia)

transitions.funFact: For a quarter of a century West German maps would not let go. Official maps and school atlases kept marking Germany's 1937 border around Silesia, Pomerania and East Prussia, lands Potsdam had placed under Polish administration until a peace treaty. The habit faded with Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik and the Treaty of Warsaw, and a 1990 treaty settled the border for good.

sources.title: Deutschland in den Grenzen vom 31. Dezember 1937 (German Wikipedia)

features.title: Angola and Mozambique: Portuguese, or independent
features.subject: Southern Africa

states.label: Both Portuguese
states.question: Are Angola and Mozambique both Portuguese?
states.cue: The two big territories on either side of southern Africa share Portugal's colour, marked (Port.) or named Portuguese West Africa and Portuguese East Africa.

states.label: Only Angola Portuguese
states.question: Is Mozambique independent while Angola is still Portuguese?
states.cue: Only Angola, on the Atlantic side, still has Portugal's colour. This lasted under five months, in 1975.

states.label: Both independent
states.question: Are Angola and Mozambique both independent?
states.cue: Both have their own colours. Mozambique's capital may read Maputo instead of Lourenço Marques.

transitions.funFact: Portugal clung to its African empire long after Britain and France had let go, fighting colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea from 1961. The Carnation Revolution in Lisbon on 25 April 1974 ended that. Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975, Cape Verde and São Tomé weeks later.

Angola became independent on 11 November 1975 in the middle of a civil war: three movements fought over Luanda, backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba on one side and the United States, Zaire and South Africa on the other. The war lasted, on and off, until 2002.

features.title: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
features.subject: South-central Africa

states.label: Three territories
states.question: Is this area split into three separate territories, not one federation?
states.cue: Three names, each with its own border: Northern and Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland before 1953, or Zambia, Rhodesia and Malawi after 1964.

states.label: One federation
states.question: Are the two Rhodesias and Nyasaland joined as one federation?
states.cue: One outline around all three, labelled Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland (Fed. of Rhod. & Nyasa.) or Central African Federation. The old borders may still show as thin lines.

fr: Fédération de Rhodésie et du Nyassaland
it: Federazione della Rhodesia e del Nyasaland
ja: ローデシア・ニヤサランド連邦

states.label: Three countries
states.question: Are Zambia, Rhodesia and Malawi three separate countries?
states.cue: Three separate countries: Zambia in the north, Rhodesia (Zimbabwe) south of the Zambezi, Malawi along Lake Malawi.

transitions.funFact: In 1953 Britain bundled Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland into one federation, sold as a "partnership" between races. Most Africans saw a white settlers' project: power sat in Salisbury, and the copper wealth of the north paid for much of the south. Its showpiece was the Kariba Dam on the Zambezi.

African opposition, led by Hastings Banda in Nyasaland and Kenneth Kaunda in Northern Rhodesia, broke the federation apart. It was dissolved on 31 December 1963; within ten months Malawi and Zambia were independent, while white-ruled Southern Rhodesia went its own way and declared independence alone in 1965.

features.title: Romania: Old Kingdom, Greater Romania, cut down in 1940, or post-war
features.subject: Romania

states.label: Old Kingdom
states.question: Is Romania a crescent around the Carpathians, without Transylvania?
states.cue: Romania wraps around the outside of the Carpathians from the Danube to the Prut; Transylvania is Hungarian (Austria-Hungary) and Bessarabia is Russian.

states.label: Greater Romania
states.question: Does Romania reach east to the Dniester, taking in Bessarabia and Transylvania?
states.cue: A big, round Romania: Transylvania in the middle, Bessarabia up to the Dniester in the east, Bukovina in the north and the southern Dobruja on the Black Sea.

depictions.label: Bessarabia Romanian
depictions.question: Does Romania reach east to the Dniester, taking in Bessarabia and Transylvania?
depictions.cue: Romania's colour runs all the way to the Dniester, as on most maps outside the Soviet Union.

depictions.label: Bessarabia hatched as occupied
depictions.question: Is Bessarabia, between the Prut and the Dniester, hatched as occupied land?
depictions.cue: Soviet maps ended Romania at the Prut and hatched Bessarabia as Romanian-occupied, with the Moldavian autonomous republic just across the Dniester.

states.label: Cut down in 1940
states.question: Does Hungary cut deep into Romania, holding northern Transylvania?
states.cue: Hungary's colour reaches across northern Transylvania almost to the Black Sea bend of the Carpathians, leaving Romania a horseshoe; Bessarabia is lost to the USSR and the southern Dobruja to Bulgaria. Maps of 1940 to 1944.

depictions.label: Northern Transylvania Hungarian
depictions.question: Does Hungary cut deep into Romania, holding northern Transylvania?
depictions.cue: The Vienna Award line drawn as a border, with Hungary north of it.

depictions.label: Transylvania still Romanian
depictions.question: Is Romania round, with Transylvania but without Bessarabia?
depictions.cue: Some Allied maps showed the Soviet gains of 1940 but ignored the German-Italian Vienna Award.

states.label: Post-war Romania
states.question: Is Romania round, with Transylvania but without Bessarabia?
states.cue: Transylvania is Romanian again, but the eastern border runs along the Prut: Bessarabia (Moldavia, later Moldova) is Soviet, and the southern Dobruja is Bulgarian.

transitions.funFact: At the end of the First World War Romania nearly doubled in size. Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania all voted to join it during 1918, and the peace treaties confirmed Greater Romania, which Soviet Russia never accepted for Bessarabia.

sources.title: Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina (Wikipedia)

transitions.funFact: Romania lost a third of its land in one summer. In June 1940 a Soviet ultimatum took Bessarabia, in August Germany and Italy awarded northern Transylvania to Hungary at Vienna, and in September Bulgaria got the southern Dobruja back.

sources.title: Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina (Wikipedia)

transitions.funFact: The 1947 peace treaty gave northern Transylvania back to Romania but kept the Soviet border of 1941, so Bessarabia stayed Soviet and became the Moldavian republic, today's Moldova. Romania's outline has not changed since.

features.title: Ruanda-Urundi, one territory or Rwanda and Burundi
features.subject: East of Lake Kivu

states.label: Part of German East Africa
states.question: Are Rwanda and Burundi part of German East Africa?
states.cue: Before the First World War this corner belongs to the big German colony to its east, labelled German East Africa (Deutsch-Ostafrika).

states.label: Ruanda-Urundi
states.question: Is it one territory called Ruanda-Urundi?
states.cue: One small territory squeezed between the Belgian Congo and Tanganyika, labelled Ruanda-Urundi and usually in Belgium's colour.

states.label: Rwanda and Burundi
states.question: Are Rwanda and Burundi two separate countries?
states.cue: Two small countries side by side: Rwanda in the north, Burundi in the south.

transitions.funFact: Belgian troops from the Congo occupied the north-western corner of German East Africa in 1916. Germany gave up its colonies when the Treaty of Versailles took effect in January 1920; Belgium kept this corner as Ruanda-Urundi, confirmed as a League of Nations mandate on 20 July 1922, while Britain took the much larger rest as Tanganyika.

Belgium ran Rwanda and Burundi as one territory for forty years, but they were two old kingdoms, and on 1 July 1962 they became independent separately. Both are among Africa's smallest and most densely populated countries, and both inherited deep divisions between Hutu and Tutsi.

features.title: Location of Russia's capital: St Petersburg (Petrograd) or Moscow
features.subject: Russia's capital

states.label: St Petersburg
states.question: Is the capital star at St Petersburg, on the Gulf of Finland?
states.cue: The star sits at St Petersburg (Petrograd from 1914) on the Baltic; Moscow, the old capital, is an ordinary big city.

states.label: Moscow
states.question: Is the capital star at Moscow, far inland?
states.cue: The star sits at Moscow (Moskau, Moscou); the city on the Gulf of Finland, now Petrograd or Leningrad, has a plain city dot.

transitions.funFact: With German armies advancing after peace talks broke down, Lenin's government slipped out of Petrograd by night train and set up in Moscow's Kremlin on 12 March 1918. It was meant to be an emergency move, but Moscow, Russia's capital before Peter the Great built his new city two centuries earlier, has been the capital ever since.

sources.title: Moscow becomes the capital of the Soviet state (Presidential Library, Russia)

features.title: Rybinsk Reservoir on the upper Volga
features.subject: Upper Volga

states.label: Only rivers
states.question: Do the rivers meet at Rybinsk with no big lake?
states.claim: The rivers simply meet at Rybinsk
states.cue: Only the Volga, Mologa and Sheksna rivers, with the town of Mologa at their meeting point.

states.label: Big reservoir
states.question: Is there a big lake north-west of Rybinsk?
states.claim: A big lake lies by Rybinsk
states.cue: A large lake, about 100 km long, spreads north-west from Rybinsk; the town of Mologa is gone.

transitions.funFact: When the dam at Rybinsk was closed in April 1941, the water rose over 4,580 km² of forest and farmland. At the time it was the largest man-made body of water on Earth. The old town of Mologa and some 660 villages vanished, and about 150,000 people were moved.

features.title: The Saar: German, under the League, or a French protectorate
features.subject: Saar

states.label: Part of Germany
states.question: Is the Saar simply part of Germany?
states.claim: The Saar is part of Germany
states.cue: No separate border: the Saar is inside Germany, next to Lorraine.

states.label: Under the League of Nations
states.question: Is the Saar a separate territory between France and Germany?
states.claim: The Saar is a separate territory
states.cue: A small territory with its own border around Saarbrücken, labelled Saar Territory, Saargebiet or Territoire du Bassin de la Sarre.

states.label: Part of Germany
states.question: Is the Saar simply part of Germany?
states.claim: The Saar is part of Germany
states.cue: No separate border: the Saar is inside Germany again (1935-45).

states.label: French protectorate
states.question: Is the Saar a separate territory between France and Germany?
states.claim: The Saar is a separate territory
states.cue: The Saar has its own border again, often tied to France by colour or a note (Saarland, Sarre, Fr.). Maps of 1947 to 1956.

states.label: Part of Germany
states.question: Is the Saar simply part of Germany?
states.claim: The Saar is part of Germany
states.cue: No separate border: the Saarland is one of the German states.

transitions.funFact: The Treaty of Versailles, in force from 10 January 1920, put the coal-rich Saar under the League of Nations for fifteen years, with its mines given to France as compensation for wrecked French pits. The people were to decide their future in a vote afterwards.

In the plebiscite of 13 January 1935, 90.8 percent of Saarlanders voted to rejoin Germany, by then ruled by Hitler. It was the Nazi regime's first territorial gain, achieved by a fair vote under League supervision.

After the war France split the Saar off as a protectorate with its own constitution, currency and even an Olympic team, which competed at Helsinki in 1952. For a few years Europe had an extra, half-independent state on the French border.

In October 1955 two thirds of Saar voters rejected a plan to make their land a European territory. France accepted the result, and on 1 January 1957 the Saarland joined West Germany as its smallest state apart from the city-states.

features.title: Sakhalin and the Kurils: who holds the south of the island and the island chain
features.subject: Sakhalin and the Kurils

states.label: Sakhalin Russian, Kurils Japanese
states.question: Is all of Sakhalin Russian, with only the Kurils in Japan's colour?
states.cue: No border across Sakhalin: the whole island is Russian, while the Kuril chain shares Japan's colour.

states.label: Sakhalin split at 50° N
states.question: Does a straight border cross Sakhalin, with the south in Japan's colour?
states.cue: A ruler-straight line crosses Sakhalin at 50° N: Karafuto in the south is Japanese, like the Kurils; the north is Russian or Soviet.

states.label: All Soviet
states.question: Are all of Sakhalin and the Kurils outside Japan's colour?
states.claim: Moscow holds Sakhalin and all the Kurils
states.cue: Sakhalin has no border across it and the whole Kuril chain is Soviet (Russian), right up to the tip of Hokkaido.

depictions.label: All Soviet
depictions.question: Are all of Sakhalin and the Kurils outside Japan's colour?
depictions.claim: Moscow holds Sakhalin and all the Kurils
depictions.cue: The whole island chain is Soviet (Russian), right up to Hokkaido.

depictions.label: Southern Kurils Japanese
depictions.question: Are the southernmost Kuril islands, next to Hokkaido, still in Japan's colour?
depictions.cue: Japanese maps colour Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islands as Japan (the Northern Territories, 北方領土) and often leave southern Sakhalin and the other Kurils white as undetermined.

transitions.funFact: After its surprise victory over Russia, Japan won the southern half of Sakhalin in the Treaty of Portsmouth, signed in the US in September 1905. The new border followed the 50th parallel exactly, a ruler-straight line cutting the island in two.

The Soviet Union attacked Karafuto on 11 August 1945, three days before Japan surrendered, and took the Kurils in the following weeks. Japan still claims the southernmost Kurils, and today's Japanese maps colour them as Japanese, a dispute that has blocked a peace treaty since the war.

features.title: Salton Sea: dry Salton Sink or an accidental lake
features.subject: Southern California

states.label: Dry Salton Sink
states.question: Is the basin south-east of Indio dry, with no lake?
states.claim: The Salton basin is dry desert
states.cue: Desert or a salt flat below sea level, marked Salton Sink, Colorado Desert or salt beds, with no lake.

states.label: Salton Sea
states.question: Is there a long lake, the Salton Sea, in the desert south-east of Indio?
states.claim: The Salton Sea is on the map
states.cue: A lake about 50 km long between Indio and the Imperial Valley farms, labelled Salton Sea.

transitions.funFact: The Salton Sea is an accident. In 1905 floods on the Colorado River burst through a poorly built irrigation intake, and for almost two years most of the river poured into the dry Salton Sink, below sea level. The Southern Pacific railroad finally plugged the breach in February 1907. The lake it left is still California's largest.

features.title: Sandy Island, the phantom island in the Coral Sea
features.subject: Coral Sea

states.label: Sandy Island shown
states.question: Is there a small island called Sandy Island in the Coral Sea, west of New Caledonia?
states.claim: Sandy Island is on the map
states.cue: A small island, about 24 km long, at 19° 13' S, 159° 56' E, labelled Sandy Island or Île de Sable.

states.label: Open sea
states.question: Is the sea west of New Caledonia empty, with no island at 19° S?
states.claim: The sea west of New Caledonia is empty
states.cue: Nothing between the Chesterfield Islands and New Caledonia at that latitude.

transitions.funFact: Sandy Island sat on maps for well over a century, even on Google Earth, until scientists on the Australian research ship Southern Surveyor sailed to it in November 2012 and found open ocean 1,300 metres deep. It was probably a raft of floating pumice or an error copied from chart to chart.

features.title: Santo Domingo or Ciudad Trujillo
features.subject: Capital of the Dominican Republic

states.label: Santo Domingo
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Santo Domingo (Saint-Domingue in French, São Domingos in Portuguese).

states.label: Ciudad Trujillo
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Ciudad Trujillo (C. Trujillo).

ja: シウダー・トルヒーヨ
シウダー・トルヒーヨ

states.label: Santo Domingo
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Santo Domingo again.

transitions.funFact: In January 1936 the dictator Rafael Trujillo had the oldest European city in the Americas, founded in 1496, renamed after himself: Ciudad Trujillo. He also named the country's highest mountain Pico Trujillo, and signs everywhere read "God and Trujillo".

Trujillo was assassinated in May 1961 after 31 years in power, and by the end of the year his name had been scraped off the map: Ciudad Trujillo became Santo Domingo again, and Pico Trujillo became Pico Duarte.

features.title: Arabia, Hejaz and Nejd, or Saudi Arabia
features.subject: Kingdom on the Arabian peninsula

states.label: Arabia
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Just Arabia (Arabien, Arabie) across the desert, with region names like Nejd and Hejaz; no single kingdom.

states.label: Hejaz and Nejd
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Hejaz and Nejd (Hedschas und Nedschd, Hedjaz et Nedjd): Ibn Saud's two kingdoms under one king. Maps of 1926 to 1932.

states.label: Saudi Arabia
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Saudi Arabia (Saudi-Arabien, Arabie saoudite), named after the ruling House of Saud.

transitions.funFact: Abdulaziz ibn Saud, ruler of the desert emirate of Nejd, conquered the Hejaz with Mecca and Medina in 1925 and was crowned its king in the Great Mosque of Mecca in January 1926. For six years his realm appeared on maps as Hejaz and Nejd.

On 23 September 1932 Ibn Saud united his lands as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, a country named after his own family, the House of Saud. Its lands now ran from the Red Sea with Mecca and Medina to the Gulf coast at al-Hasa and Qatif.

features.title: The Saudi Arabia-Yemen border across the Empty Quarter: undefined or settled
features.subject: Saudi Arabia and Yemen

states.label: Undefined in the desert
states.question: Is the eastern part of the border dashed, dotted or missing?
states.claim: Part of the border is dashed or missing
states.cue: East of Najran the line is dashed or dotted, often labelled "undefined" or "indefinite boundary", or simply stops in the sand. Older maps put it in different places.

states.label: Solid all the way
states.question: Is the border a solid line all the way from the Red Sea to Oman?
states.claim: The border is solid all the way
states.cue: Since the 2000 treaty the whole border is drawn as a firm line, running north-east through the desert to the meeting point with Oman.

transitions.funFact: For 66 years nobody knew exactly where Saudi Arabia ended and Yemen began in the Empty Quarter, the world's largest sand sea, and maps simply let the line trail off. After oil was found there, the two finally drew it in 2000, keeping a 20-kilometre strip on each side where herders may still graze across the border.

features.title: Name of the city on the Irtysh beside the Soviet nuclear test site
features.subject: City on the Irtysh, Kazakhstan

states.label: Semipalatinsk
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Semipalatinsk, the Russian name, on maps from the 1700s until 2007.

states.label: Semey
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Semey (Semei, Semej), the Kazakh name, official since June 2007.

transitions.funFact: For forty years the Soviet Union set off 456 nuclear tests on the steppe west of Semipalatinsk. In 2007 Kazakhstan's president gave the city its Kazakh name, Semey, saying the old one scared off investors. A century before the bombs, Dostoevsky served five years of his Siberian exile here as a soldier.

sources.title: Kazakhs change name of city linked to nuke tests (RFE/RL, 21 June 2007)

features.title: Senegambia: Senegal and the Gambia as one confederation
features.subject: Senegal and the Gambia

states.label: Two countries
states.question: Are Senegal and the Gambia shown as two separate countries?
states.claim: Senegal and the Gambia are separate
states.cue: Two names and two colours: the Gambia is a thin strip along its river, surrounded by Senegal on three sides.

states.label: Senegambia
states.question: Are Senegal and the Gambia joined under the name Senegambia?
states.claim: Senegal and the Gambia are Senegambia
states.cue: One name, Senegambia (Sénégambie), spans both countries, often in one colour, with the Gambia's outline kept as an inner or dashed line.

states.label: Two countries
states.question: Are Senegal and the Gambia shown as two separate countries?
states.claim: Senegal and the Gambia are separate
states.cue: Two names and two colours: the Gambia is a thin strip along its river, surrounded by Senegal on three sides.

transitions.funFact: In July 1981, while the Gambia's president was in London for the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana, rebels seized much of Banjul. Senegalese troops crushed the coup within days, and the shaken neighbours agreed to merge their armies and foreign policy as the Senegambia Confederation.

Senegambia never got the planned common currency or customs union: the Gambia feared being swallowed by a neighbour almost twenty times its size. When it refused to move closer to a full union, Senegal dissolved the confederation on 30 September 1989, after only seven and a half years.

features.title: Severnaya Zemlya: open sea, a half-charted land, or an archipelago
features.subject: Arctic Ocean north of Siberia

states.label: Open sea
states.question: Is there only open sea north of the Taymyr peninsula?
states.claim: There is only sea north of Taymyr
states.cue: The Kara and Laptev Seas run together north of Cape Chelyuskin, with no land beyond Asia's northernmost cape.

states.label: One half-charted land
states.question: Is there one large land north of the Taymyr peninsula, with its western coast left unfinished?
states.claim: One large land lies north of Taymyr
states.cue: Emperor Nicholas II Land (from 1926 Severnaya Zemlya), drawn from its south-eastern coast only, often as one land with a dotted or open western side.

states.label: An archipelago
states.question: Is there a group of large islands north of the Taymyr peninsula, split by straits?
states.cue: Severnaya Zemlya (Northern Land) as four main islands with straits between them.

ja: セヴェルナヤ・ゼムリャ

transitions.funFact: The last large land on Earth to be found turned up only in September 1913, when Boris Vilkitsky's icebreakers Taymyr and Vaygach tried to sail the Northern Sea Route. Nordenskiöld and Nansen had sailed past without seeing it. Russia named it Emperor Nicholas II Land; the Soviets renamed it Severnaya Zemlya, 'Northern Land', in 1926.

For nearly twenty years nobody knew the land's western half. Then Georgy Ushakov and Nikolay Urvantsev spent two years on it from 1930 with dog sleds and found not one land but four big islands, which they named October Revolution, Bolshevik, Komsomolets and Pioneer.

features.title: Siam (Thailand): how far east and south its borders reach
features.subject: Siam

states.label: Beyond the Mekong
states.question: Does Siam reach east beyond the Mekong, across Laos towards the mountains of Annam?
states.cue: Siam's colour covers most of Laos east of the Mekong; French Indochina is only the coastal strip of Annam and Tonkin, Cochinchina and Cambodia.

states.label: Mekong border, Angkor Siamese
states.question: Does Siam end at the Mekong, but still hold Angkor and the land around Battambang?
states.claim: Siam ends at the Mekong, with Angkor
states.cue: The Mekong is the border with French Laos for most of its length; Battambang, Siem Reap and the Angkor temples are Siamese, and so is the Malay peninsula down to Kedah and Kelantan.

states.label: Angkor Cambodian, long southern tail
states.question: Is Angkor in French Cambodia, while Siam still reaches far down the Malay peninsula?
states.cue: Cambodia wraps around the Tonle Sap lake and holds Angkor, but Siam's southern tail still includes Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu.

states.label: Today's outline
states.question: Does Siam have today's outline, with Angkor in Cambodia and Kedah and Kelantan in Malaya?
states.cue: Today's Thailand: Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu belong to British Malaya (later Malaysia), Angkor to Cambodia, and Laos lies across the Mekong.

states.label: Wartime gains
states.question: Does Thailand again hold western Cambodia, the Lao lands west of the Mekong and the northern Malay states?
states.cue: Thailand drawn with its wartime gains: Battambang and Siem Reap, the Lao provinces on the Mekong's west bank and, later, Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu.

depictions.label: With wartime gains
depictions.question: Does Siam end at the Mekong, but still hold Angkor and the land around Battambang?
depictions.claim: Siam ends at the Mekong, with Angkor
depictions.cue: Thailand drawn with its wartime gains, which give it nearly its outline of the 1890s again.

depictions.label: Gains not shown
depictions.question: Does Siam have today's outline, with Angkor in Cambodia and Kedah and Kelantan in Malaya?
depictions.cue: The pre-war border, as most maps outside Thailand and Japan kept drawing it.

states.label: Today's outline
states.question: Does Siam have today's outline, with Angkor in Cambodia and Kedah and Kelantan in Malaya?
states.cue: Today's Thailand: Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu belong to Malaysia, Angkor to Cambodia, and Laos lies across the Mekong.

transitions.funFact: In July 1893 two French gunboats forced their way past the forts at Paknam and anchored in Bangkok with their guns trained on the Grand Palace. France demanded everything east of the Mekong, and the treaty of 3 October 1893 handed it Laos, about a fifth of the land Siam then claimed. French troops held Chanthaburi as a pledge.

Angkor Wat changed hands on paper in 1907. Siam had ruled Battambang and Siem Reap, the provinces around the temples, since the 1790s. A treaty of 23 March 1907 gave them to French Cambodia in return for Trat, a coastal province French troops had been holding, and Cambodians still celebrate the return of Angkor.

Siam's long southern tail shrank in 1909, when it handed Kedah, Kelantan, Terengganu and Perlis to Britain, which added them to British Malaya. In return most British subjects in Siam lost their right to be tried in British consular courts, and Siam got a loan to build its railway south. The four states are part of Malaysia today.

After a short border war with Vichy France, Thailand won back western Cambodia and the Lao lands west of the Mekong in a treaty brokered by Japan and signed in Tokyo on 9 May 1941. In 1943 Japan added four Malay states and two Shan states. Bangkok built its Victory Monument; the gains lasted barely five years.

Thailand gave the Malay states back to Britain in 1945, but France kept blocking its entry to the United Nations until it also returned the lands taken from Indochina. The settlement signed in Washington on 17 November 1946 restored the 1907 border, and Thailand joined the UN that December.

features.title: Horn of Africa: British Somaliland alone, British and Italian Somaliland, or one Somalia
features.subject: Horn of Africa

states.label: British Somaliland only
states.question: Is only the north coast in a colonial colour, with no Italian territory on the Indian Ocean coast?
states.claim: Only the north coast is colonial
states.cue: British Somaliland (Somali Coast Protectorate) on the Gulf of Aden; the long east coast uncoloured, labelled Somali Land, or with Mogadishu and Brava marked as the Sultan of Zanzibar's ports.

ja: イギリス領ソマリランド

states.label: Two Somalilands
states.question: Are British and Italian Somaliland two separate territories?
states.claim: British and Italian Somaliland are split
states.cue: The north coast (British Somaliland, capital Hargeisa) and the long Indian Ocean coast (Italian Somaliland, capital Mogadishu) have different colours and names.

ja: イギリス領ソマリランド
イタリア領ソマリランド

states.label: One Somalia
states.question: Is Somalia one country around the whole Horn of Africa?
states.cue: One country, Somalia, from the Gulf of Aden round the Horn to Kenya, with Mogadishu as its capital.

transitions.funFact: Italy built its Somali colony by treaty rather than conquest: in 1889 the sultans of Hobyo and Majeerteen accepted Italian protection on condition that Italy stayed out of their affairs. Mogadishu and the other Benadir ports still answered to the Sultan of Zanzibar, and Italian troops only moved in there in 1893. The colony reached the Juba River in 1925.

British Somaliland became independent on 26 June 1960 and joined the former Italian Somaliland five days later, on 1 July, to form the Somali Republic. Since 1991 the north has run itself again as Somaliland, which no country recognises, so most maps still draw one Somalia.

features.title: Southern Africa: Boer republics, four British colonies, or the Union of South Africa
features.subject: Southern Africa

states.label: Two Boer republics
states.question: Are the Transvaal and the Orange Free State independent Boer republics, beside British Cape Colony and Natal?
states.cue: Two inland republics in colours of their own, labelled South African Republic (Transvaal, Z.A.R.) and Orange Free State (Oranje-Vrijstaat), ringed by British territory.

states.label: Four British colonies
states.question: Are the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony four separate British colonies?
states.cue: Four colonies with borders between them, all in Britain's colour; the Orange Free State is now the Orange River Colony (O.R.C.).

states.label: One Union of South Africa
states.question: Is South Africa one country, the Union of South Africa, from the Cape to the Limpopo?
states.cue: One label across the four former colonies: Union of South Africa (Zuid-Afrikaansche Unie, Südafrikanische Union), later Republic of South Africa. Thin province lines may remain inside it.

transitions.funFact: Britain declared both Boer republics annexed in 1900, after taking their capitals, but the Boers fought on as guerrillas for two more years, and Britain answered with scorched earth and concentration camps. Only the Peace of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902 ended the war, and the republics became the Transvaal and Orange River colonies.

Eight years to the day after Vereeniging, the four colonies became the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910. Unable to agree on one capital, the new country took three: Pretoria for the government, Cape Town for parliament and Bloemfontein for the courts, a split South Africa still keeps today.

features.title: Sudan: one country or two
features.subject: Sudan

states.label: One Sudan
states.question: Is Sudan one big country, stretching from Egypt down to Uganda and Kenya?
states.cue: One Sudan, Africa's largest country, reaching from the Egyptian border to the forests of the south. Before 1956 it is the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan.

states.label: Sudan and South Sudan
states.question: Is Sudan split in two, with South Sudan below a border across the middle?
states.cue: Two countries: Sudan in the north, around Khartoum, and South Sudan in the south, around Juba.

transitions.funFact: After two long civil wars, 98.8% of southern voters chose independence in a referendum in January 2011, and South Sudan became the world's newest country on 9 July 2011. Its birth also cost Sudan the title of Africa's largest country, which passed to Algeria.

features.title: Soviet Union: one country or fifteen
features.subject: Russia and its neighbours

states.label: One huge country
states.question: Is it one single country from the Baltic to the Pacific, with no borders across it?
states.claim: It is one country to the Pacific
states.cue: One country: the Russian Empire until 1917 and the Soviet Union (U.S.S.R., СССР) from 1922. Internal republic boundaries are at most thin lines.

states.label: Fifteen countries
states.question: Is it split into Russia and many neighbours, such as Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan, each with its own border?
states.claim: It is Russia and many neighbours
states.cue: Fifteen countries: Russia, the three Baltic states, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, three in the Caucasus and five in Central Asia.

transitions.funFact: After a failed coup in Moscow in August 1991, the Soviet republics declared independence one after another. On 25 December Mikhail Gorbachev resigned, the red flag over the Kremlin was lowered that evening, and on 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union formally ceased to exist, leaving fifteen countries in its place.

transitions.funFact: Spain lost the last of its American empire in one summer. The United States declared war in April 1898, two months after the battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour, and the fighting was over by August. In the Treaty of Paris Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. Spaniards still call 1898 simply "the Disaster".

American troops ran Cuba for more than three years after Spain left. They withdrew on 20 May 1902, but only after Cuba wrote the Platt Amendment into its constitution, giving the United States a right to intervene and land for naval bases. One of them, Guantánamo Bay, leased in 1903, is still American today.

features.title: Name of Russia's city at the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland
features.subject: City on the Gulf of Finland

ja: サンクトペテルブルク

states.label: Petrograd
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Renamed in 1914 because 'Petersburg' sounded too German during the war.

states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: The name from 1924 to 1991. No capital star: Moscow is the capital.

states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: The old name came back in 1991.

ja: サンクトペテルブルク
サンクトペテルブルク

transitions.funFact: When war with Germany broke out in 1914, the German-sounding Sankt-Peterburg was replaced by the more Russian Petrograd, on 31 August (18 August in the old Russian calendar). Both names mean 'Peter's city'. Four years later the Bolsheviks also moved the capital to Moscow.
Lenin died on 21 January 1924, and five days later the city was renamed Leningrad in his honour. It kept that name through the 872-day siege of the Second World War and the rest of the Soviet era.

In a June 1991 referendum a narrow majority of residents voted to bring back the original name, and the city officially became Saint Petersburg again on 6 September 1991. The region around it is still called Leningrad Oblast today.

features.title: Spitsbergen: no man's land or Norwegian (Svalbard)

states.label: Norwegian
states.question: Is Spitsbergen (Svalbard) in Norway's colour?
states.cue: The islands share Norway's colour, often labelled Svalbard or Spitsbergen (Norw.).

ja: スヴァールバル（ノルウェー）

transitions.funFact: For three centuries Spitsbergen belonged to nobody: whalers, trappers and later coal miners from many countries came and went. The 1920 treaty gave it to Norway, but every signatory may still mine and fish there, which is why Russia runs a coal town, Barentsburg. Norway took over on 14 August 1925 and renamed it Svalbard.

transitions.funFact: Norway shared a king and a foreign ministry with Sweden from 1814, but kept its own parliament, army and money. On 7 June 1905 the Storting declared the union over because the king could no longer form a government. A referendum backed it by 368,208 votes to 184, and a Danish prince became King Haakon VII.

features.title: Taiwan (Formosa): Chinese, Japanese, or a separate Republic of China
features.subject: Taiwan

states.label: In China's colour
states.question: Is Taiwan in the same colour as mainland China?
states.cue: The island shares China's colour, as a Chinese province, often labelled Formosa.

states.label: In Japan's colour
states.question: Is Taiwan in Japan's colour?
states.cue: Formosa (台湾) is coloured like Japan, linked to it through the Ryukyu Islands; mainland China is a different colour.

states.label: In China's colour
states.question: Is Taiwan in the same colour as mainland China?
states.cue: The island is Chinese again and shares the mainland's colour. Maps of 1945 to 1949.

states.label: Separate Republic of China
states.question: Does Taiwan have its own colour, apart from mainland China?
states.cue: Taiwan has a colour of its own, labelled Republic of China, Nationalist China or Taiwan (Formosa), with the capital Taipei.

depictions.label: Own colour
depictions.question: Does Taiwan have its own colour, apart from mainland China?
depictions.cue: A separate colour and its own name, Republic of China or Taiwan.

depictions.label: China's colour
depictions.question: Is Taiwan in the same colour as mainland China?
depictions.cue: Soviet-bloc maps, and maps following Beijing's view, colour Taiwan like the mainland as a province of China.

transitions.funFact: China ceded Formosa to Japan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki after losing the war of 1894-95. Local leaders declared a Republic of Formosa in May 1895 to resist, but Japanese troops took its last stronghold, Tainan, that October and ruled the island for fifty years.
After Japan's surrender, the Republic of China took over the island on 25 October 1945. Fifty years of Japanese rule ended, and Formosa disappeared from maps in Japan's colour almost overnight.

Losing the civil war, Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan on 7 December 1949 and made Taipei its capital. Both governments claimed to be all of China, so maps split: most Western atlases gave Taiwan its own colour, Soviet-bloc ones coloured it like the mainland.

sources.title: Retreat of the government of the Republic of China to Taiwan (Wikipedia)

features.title: Name of Estonia's capital: Reval or Tallinn
features.subject: Port on the Gulf of Finland

states.label: Reval
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: The German and Swedish name, used on most maps while Estonia was part of Russia.

states.label: Tallinn
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: The Estonian name, printed as the capital of independent Estonia; German maps long kept Reval.

transitions.funFact: For seven centuries Germans, Swedes and Russians called the town Reval, after an old Estonian county. Independent Estonia used its own name, Tallinn, usually explained as Taani linn, 'Danish castle', after the fortress the Danes built there after conquering it in 1219. Foreign maps took a few years to follow.

features.title: German East Africa, Tanganyika or Tanzania
features.subject: South of Lake Victoria

states.label: German East Africa
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: A German colony: Deutsch-Ostafrika, German East Africa.

states.label: Tanganyika
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Tanganyika (Territory), British-run from 1920, independent 1961–64.

states.label: Tanzania
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Tanzania, including the islands of Zanzibar and Pemba.

transitions.funFact: Britain took most of German East Africa in the First World War and named it Tanganyika Territory, after the long lake on its western border. The explorers Burton and Speke had been the first Europeans to see that lake, in 1858.

Months after a revolution on Zanzibar, mainland Tanganyika and the islands united in April 1964. The clumsy "United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar" was replaced on 29 October by Tanzania, a blend of the two names reportedly picked from a public naming competition.

features.title: Tiflis or Tbilisi
features.subject: Capital of Georgia

states.label: Tiflis
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Tiflis (Тифлис, チフリス), the Russian and Western form until 1936.

states.label: Tbilisi
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Tbilisi (Tbilissi, Тбилиси), closer to the Georgian name.

transitions.funFact: The name means "warm place", after the sulphur springs the city is built around. On 17 August 1936 the Soviet leadership changed the official Russian form from Tiflis to Tbilisi, closer to Georgian; Western atlases followed slowly, and German, Spanish and Turkish still say Tiflis.

features.title: Siam or Thailand
features.subject: Kingdom between Burma and Indochina

states.label: Siam
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Siam (Sião, Syjam), the name used abroad until 1939.

states.label: Thailand
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Thailand (Thaïlande, Tailandia, タイ). Maps of 1939 to 1945.

states.label: Siam
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Siam again, on maps of 1945 to 1949.

states.label: Thailand
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Thailand, used since 1949.

transitions.funFact: On 24 June 1939 the military strongman Phibun changed the country's official English name from Siam to Thailand, urged on by his nationalist adviser Wichit. War broke out weeks later, and few maps were printed before the name changed back.

Thailand had sided with Japan in the war. After the defeat, the new civilian government led by Seni Pramoj dropped the wartime name and went back to Siam in September 1945, distancing the country from Phibun's nationalism.

sources.title: Bangkok Post, Thailand Journey timeline: 11 May 1949, Siam officially renamed Thailand

transitions.funFact: On the evening of 11 May 1949 Radio Bangkok announced that the country's official name would return to Thailand, after months of fierce debate between nationalists and liberal intellectuals. The name has stayed ever since.
