features.title: Goiás split: the new state of Tocantins
features.subject: States of central Brazil

states.label: One Goiás
states.question: Is Goiás one tall state, reaching far north towards the Amazon?
states.cue: A single state, Goiás, from the Federal District around Brasília northwards about 1,500 km, with no Tocantins.

states.label: Tocantins split off
states.question: Is there a separate state, Tocantins, north of Goiás?
states.cue: A border runs east–west across the old Goiás at about 13° S: Goiás in the south, Tocantins in the north with its capital Palmas.

transitions.funFact: Brazil's 1988 constitution cut the northern two-fifths off Goiás and made it Tocantins, named after its river ("toucan's beak" in Tupi). Its capital, Palmas, was built from nothing on former farmland and was planned for a million people.

features.title: Tucuruí reservoir on the Tocantins
features.subject: Lower Tocantins, eastern Amazon

states.label: Just the river
states.question: Is the Tocantins an ordinary river here, with no big lake?
states.claim: The Tocantins is an ordinary river
states.cue: A single river line running north towards Belém through the forest.

states.label: Tucuruí lake
states.question: Does the Tocantins widen into a long, branching lake?
states.claim: The Tocantins widens into a lake
states.cue: A long lake with many ragged arms and islands behind the Tucuruí dam, labelled Tucuruí or Represa de Tucuruí.

transitions.funFact: Tucuruí was the first giant dam in the Brazilian Amazon, built mainly to power aluminium smelters. Its lake drowned a long stretch of rainforest, and 25,000 to 35,000 people had to leave; 3,750 of them were resettled on new islands that the rising water had created.

features.title: Location of Turkey's capital: Constantinople or Angora (Ankara)
features.subject: Turkey's capital

states.label: Constantinople
states.question: Is the capital star at Constantinople, on the Bosporus?
states.cue: The Ottoman Empire's star sits at Constantinople (Konstantinopel, Cařihrad); Angora is a small inland town.

states.label: Angora (Ankara)
states.question: Is the capital star at Angora (Ankara), in the middle of Anatolia?
states.cue: The star sits at Angora, later spelled Ankara, on the central plateau; the city on the Bosporus is an ordinary city.

transitions.funFact: Mustafa Kemal ran the war of independence from Angora, a small Anatolian town on the railway, out of reach of the Allied warships at Constantinople. On 13 October 1923 the Grand National Assembly made it the capital of the new Turkey. A year later it had only about 35,000 people.

features.title: English name of Turkey
features.subject: Country on the Bosporus

states.label: Turkey
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Turkey, the English name used for the Ottoman Empire on many old maps and for the Republic since 1923.

states.label: Türkiye
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Türkiye, the Turkish form the government asked the world to use from 2022.

transitions.funFact: Turkey asked the United Nations to call it Türkiye, and the UN agreed on 1 June 2022. The government said the Turkish name best expresses the nation's culture and values; it also stops the country sharing a name with a bird. Most maps outside English still use local names such as Türkei or Turquie.

features.title: Tuva: Chinese, Russian, Tannu Tuva, or Soviet
features.subject: North of Mongolia

states.label: Part of China (Mongolia)
states.question: Is the land north-west of Mongolia part of China?
states.claim: The land by Mongolia is Chinese
states.cue: The basin is part of China's Mongolian lands, sometimes labelled Uriankhai; Russia's border runs along the Sayan mountains to the north.

states.label: Russian / Soviet colour
states.question: Is Tuva inside Russia's (or the Soviet Union's) colour?
states.cue: Russia's colour comes down to Mongolia's border; Tuva is at most a region name.

states.label: Tannu Tuva
states.question: Is there a separate country, Tannu Tuva, north-west of Mongolia?
states.cue: A small country with its own colour and border between Mongolia and Siberia, labelled Tannu Tuva, Tuva or Tuwa, capital Kyzyl.

states.label: Russian / Soviet colour
states.question: Is Tuva inside Russia's (or the Soviet Union's) colour?
states.cue: The Soviet (later Russian) colour reaches down to Mongolia's border; Tuva is an autonomous region.

transitions.funFact: Tuva had been part of Mongolia under the Qing dynasty since 1759. When the Chinese empire fell, Russia stepped in and in 1914 declared a protectorate over the region, then called Uriankhai, and Russian settlers moved into its valleys.

In August 1921, with Soviet backing, Tuva declared itself the Tannu Tuva People's Republic. Only the Soviet Union and Mongolia ever recognised it, but its large, colourful stamps made it famous with collectors, including the physicist Richard Feynman.

In 1944, in the middle of the war, Tuva quietly asked to join the Soviet Union, and Moscow accepted on 11 October. It became an autonomous region of the Russian republic on 1 November, and Tannu Tuva, recognised by only two states, slipped off the map.

features.title: Name of Mongolia's capital: Urga or Ulan Bator
features.subject: Mongolia's capital

states.label: Urga
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: The western name for the monastery town the Mongols called Ikh Khüree; Chinese maps say Kulun.

states.label: Ulan Bator
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: 'Red Hero', the name of the communist capital; English maps later spell it Ulaanbaatar.

transitions.funFact: The Mongolian capital began as a travelling monastery town that moved many times before settling on the Tuul River. Westerners called it Urga, Mongols Ikh Khüree, 'great camp'. In 1924 the new People's Republic renamed it Ulaanbaatar, 'Red Hero', usually linked to the revolutionary leader Sükhbaatar.

features.title: Egypt and Syria joined as the United Arab Republic
features.subject: Egypt and Syria

states.label: Two countries
states.question: Are Egypt and Syria two separate countries?
states.cue: Egypt and Syria have different colours and their own names. (Between 1961 and 1971 Egypt alone may still be labelled United Arab Republic.)

states.label: One United Arab Republic
states.question: Are Egypt and Syria joined as one country, the United Arab Republic?
states.claim: Egypt and Syria are one country
states.cue: Both are in the same colour and labelled United Arab Republic (U.A.R., R.A.U., VAR), with Israel and Jordan in between.

states.label: Two countries
states.question: Are Egypt and Syria two separate countries?
states.cue: Syria has its own colour again. Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic until 1971.

transitions.funFact: Syrian leaders, afraid of a communist takeover, flew to Cairo and asked Nasser for a union. The United Arab Republic was born in February 1958: one country in two pieces, with Israel and Jordan in between. Nasser was its president and Cairo its capital.

Syrians soon felt they were being run from Cairo, and on 28 September 1961 army officers in Damascus took Syria back out of the union. Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic for another ten years, so maps of the 1960s still print U.A.R. over Egypt alone.

features.title: Name of the country from the Baltic to the Pacific: Russia or the USSR
features.subject: Largest country

states.label: Russia
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Russia, or the Russian Empire, before the Soviet Union was founded.

states.label: USSR
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, printed in full, as initials (USSR, URSS, UdSSR, СССР) or as Soviet Union.

states.label: Russia (since 1991)
states.question: Is the country called {name}?
states.cue: Russia again, now one of fifteen countries.

transitions.funFact: On 30 December 1922 Soviet Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the Transcaucasian republic joined in a Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. It was a country name with no place and no people in it, just councils ('soviets') of workers, so that in theory any land in the world could one day join.

sources.title: Treaty on the Creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (Wikipedia)

transitions.funFact: Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991, the red flag came down over the Kremlin that evening, and the next day the Soviet Union voted itself out of existence. Russia, the largest of the fifteen successor states, took over the Soviet seat on the UN Security Council and the old name of the whole.

sources.title: Treaty on the Creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (Wikipedia)

features.title: Izhevsk, briefly Ustinov
features.subject: Capital of Udmurtia

states.label: Izhevsk
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Izhevsk (Ижевск).

states.label: Ustinov
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Ustinov (Устинов), the name used from December 1984 to June 1987.

states.label: Izhevsk
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Izhevsk again, as before 1984.

transitions.funFact: Izhevsk, a city of 600,000 that makes the Kalashnikov rifle, was renamed after the Soviet defence minister Dmitry Ustinov on 27 December 1984, a week after his death. The idea came from party officials, not from the townspeople.

Under glasnost the people of Ustinov protested openly against their new name, and on 19 June 1987, after only two and a half years, Izhevsk got its name back. As a consolation, one district of the city was named Ustinovsky.

features.title: Name of the island chain west of Fiji
features.subject: Islands west of Fiji

states.label: New Hebrides
states.question: Are the islands called {name}?
states.cue: The New Hebrides (Nouvelles-Hébrides), named by Captain Cook in 1774; an Anglo-French condominium from 1906.

ja: ニューヘブリディーズ諸島
ニューヘブリディーズ諸島

states.label: Vanuatu
states.question: Are the islands called {name}?
states.cue: Vanuatu, independent since July 1980.

transitions.funFact: For 74 years Britain and France ran the New Hebrides together, with two police forces, two school systems, two currencies and even two prisons; locals called it the Pandemonium. On 30 July 1980 the islands became independent as Vanuatu, 'land that stands up', after a short secessionist revolt on Espiritu Santo.

features.title: French Indochina, two Vietnams, or one Vietnam
features.subject: Vietnam

states.label: French Indochina
states.question: Is the whole region (Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia) one French colony?
states.claim: The region is one French colony
states.cue: One French colour covers everything east of Thailand, labelled French Indochina (Indochine française), sometimes split into Tonkin, Annam, Cochinchina, Laos and Cambodia.

ja: フランス領インドシナ

states.label: North and South Vietnam
states.question: Are there two Vietnams, North and South?
states.cue: Vietnam is cut in two at the 17th parallel, near Huế: North Vietnam (capital Hanoi) and South Vietnam (capital Saigon). Laos and Cambodia are separate countries.

states.label: One Vietnam
states.question: Is Vietnam one country from China to the Mekong delta?
states.cue: One long S-shaped Vietnam with its capital at Hanoi; Saigon is renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

transitions.funFact: The French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954 ended their Indochina War. At Geneva, Vietnam was split "temporarily" at the 17th parallel, with elections promised for 1956. They never happened, and the line became the border between communist North and American-backed South Vietnam.

North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon on 30 April 1975, and on 2 July 1976 the two halves were formally united as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City the same day, after the revolutionary leader who had died in 1969.

lookalikes.note: Vietnam drawn as one inside Indochina before 1954

features.title: Tsaritsyn, Stalingrad or Volgograd
features.subject: City on the lower Volga

states.label: Tsaritsyn
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Tsaritsyn (Zarizyn, Tsaritsyne).

states.label: Stalingrad
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Stalingrad (Stalingrado), the name made famous by the battle of 1942–43.

states.label: Volgograd
states.question: Is the city called {name}?
states.cue: Volgograd (Wolgograd).

transitions.funFact: Tsaritsyn was renamed Stalingrad in 1925 to honour Stalin's part in defending it during the Civil War. Seventeen years later the name became famous worldwide: the Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to February 1943, was the turning point of the war in Europe.

Khrushchev's campaign against Stalin's memory peaked in late 1961: Stalin's body was removed from Lenin's mausoleum, and on 10 November Stalingrad became Volgograd, "Volga city". Paris still has a Stalingrad metro station, and the city may use its wartime name on memorial days.

features.title: Walvis Bay: British, South African, or Namibian
features.subject: Port on the Namib coast

states.label: British enclave
states.question: Is Walvis Bay marked as British, (Br.)?
states.cue: A small enclave around the port, marked Walvis Bay or Walfish Bay (Br.), inside German South West Africa.

states.label: South African enclave
states.question: Is Walvis Bay marked as South African, (S. Afr.)?
states.cue: The enclave around the port is marked (S. Afr.) or in South Africa's colour.

states.label: Part of Namibia
states.question: Is Walvis Bay an ordinary Namibian town?
states.cue: No enclave: Walvis Bay is a Namibian port like any other.

transitions.funFact: Britain annexed Walvis Bay in 1878 to keep the only good harbour on the Namib coast out of other hands; it was run from Cape Town. When the Cape joined the Union of South Africa in 1910, the enclave went with it, surrounded by German South West Africa.

Walvis Bay, Namibia's only deep-water port, stayed South African for four years after Namibian independence in 1990. As apartheid ended, South Africa handed it over at midnight on 28 February 1994, together with a dozen small offshore islands.

features.title: Western Sahara: Spanish, partitioned, or Moroccan
features.subject: Atlantic Sahara

states.label: Spanish Sahara
states.question: Is the Western Sahara a Spanish colony?
states.claim: Western Sahara is a Spanish colony
states.cue: The desert coast south of Morocco is in Spain's colour, labelled Spanish Sahara, Río de Oro or Sahara Español.

states.label: Split with Mauritania
states.question: Is the Western Sahara split between Morocco and Mauritania?
states.claim: Western Sahara is split in two
states.cue: A line runs across the former Spanish Sahara: the northern two-thirds in Morocco's colour, the southern third in Mauritania's.

states.label: Held by Morocco
states.question: Is the Western Sahara shown as a separate, disputed territory?
states.cue: Since 1979 Morocco holds almost all of it. Most maps give it its own outline (dashed along Morocco), the label Western Sahara and no country's colour; Moroccan maps include it in Morocco.

depictions.label: Separate territory
depictions.question: Is the Western Sahara shown as a separate, disputed territory?
depictions.cue: Its own outline (often dashed along Morocco's border), the label Western Sahara, and no country's colour or stripes.

depictions.label: Part of Morocco
depictions.question: Is the Western Sahara drawn as part of Morocco?
depictions.claim: Western Sahara is part of Morocco
depictions.cue: No border south of Morocco: Morocco's colour runs all the way down to Mauritania. Moroccan and some Arab maps show it this way.

transitions.funFact: In November 1975, as Franco lay dying, 350,000 unarmed Moroccans marched into the Spanish Sahara in the Green March. Spain gave in and left in February 1976, and Morocco and Mauritania divided the territory between them. The Polisario Front declared a Sahrawi republic the day after Spain left.

Mauritania could not hold its third against Polisario guerrillas, who even shelled its capital, Nouakchott. It gave up its claim on 5 August 1979 and Morocco moved in. In the 1980s Morocco built a 2,700 km sand wall, the Berm, across the territory, and the dispute is still unresolved.

transitions.funFact: Besieged as a fortress city, Breslau held out for three months, surrendering only two days before the end of the war, half destroyed. Its Germans were expelled and Poles moved in, many from Lwów in the east. Today little bronze dwarfs, born of 1980s anti-communist protests, hide all over its streets.

transitions.funFact: Yellow fever killed most of the Europeans in Grand-Bassam in 1899, so the French moved the capital to a breezy hill above the lagoon and named the new town after Louis-Gustave Binger, the explorer who had been the colony's first governor.

Abidjan was a fishing village on the Ébrié Lagoon until the railway to the north started there and a wharf made it the colony's port. A decree of August 1933 made it the capital, and the offices moved from Bingerville the following summer.

President Félix Houphouët-Boigny made his home village, Yamoussoukro, the capital in March 1983. He gave it six-lane boulevards, a palace with a crocodile lake, and the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, modelled on St Peter's in Rome and claimed to be the largest church in the world.

transitions.funFact: In July 1918 Tsar Nicholas II and his family were shot in the cellar of a merchant's house in Yekaterinburg. In 1924 the city was renamed Sverdlovsk after Yakov Sverdlov, the Bolshevik leader widely believed to have approved the killings. The Church on the Blood now stands where the house was.

In September 1991, weeks after the failed coup in Moscow, the city took back its original name, given in 1723 in honour of Empress Catherine I, wife of Peter the Great. The surrounding region kept the Soviet name: it is still Sverdlovsk Oblast today.

states.cue: North Yemen (capital Sana'a) and South Yemen (capital Aden) are separate countries, sometimes labelled Y.A.R. and P.D.R.Y.

states.label: One Yemen
states.question: Is Yemen one country?
states.cue: One Yemen across the whole south-west of Arabia, with its capital at Sana'a.

transitions.funFact: When the Ottoman Empire lost the First World War, its garrisons left Yemen in November 1918 and Imam Yahya declared an independent kingdom from Sana'a. Britain kept Aden and the protectorate around it in the south, so the corner of Arabia stayed split in two.

After years of insurgency in Aden, Britain withdrew and South Yemen became independent on 30 November 1967. It soon renamed itself the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen, the only Marxist state the Arab world has had, while the north had become a republic after a 1962 coup.

On 22 May 1990 North and South Yemen merged into the Republic of Yemen, with Sana'a as its capital. It was one of the few unifications at the end of the Cold War, along with Germany's a few months later.

transitions.funFact: On 1 December 1918 the South Slav lands of the collapsed Austro-Hungarian Empire joined Serbia and Montenegro in a new kingdom of about twelve million people, with Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim communities and two alphabets. For seventy years it would be the biggest country in the Balkans.

Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and war followed in Croatia and later in Bosnia. When the European Community recognised the two new countries on 15 January 1992, Yugoslavia's break-up became official; Bosnia and Herzegovina followed in March and April 1992.

transitions.funFact: On 1 December 1918 Prince Regent Alexander proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in Belgrade, uniting Serbia and Montenegro with the South Slav lands of Austria-Hungary. It officially became Yugoslavia, 'land of the South Slavs', in 1929, but many maps used that name from the start.

After Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia left in 1991 and 1992, Serbia and Montenegro kept the name Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for another decade. On 4 February 2003 the federation renamed itself Serbia and Montenegro, and the name Yugoslavia, used since 1929, vanished from the map.

When Montenegro voted to leave in May 2006, Serbia simply carried on as the successor state: on 5 June 2006 its parliament declared the Republic of Serbia, keeping the union's seat at the United Nations. Serbia and Montenegro had lasted just three years and four months.

transitions.funFact: Northern Rhodesia, named after Cecil Rhodes, became independent on 24 October 1964 as Zambia, after the Zambezi River. It happened during the Tokyo Olympics: its team marched into the opening ceremony as Northern Rhodesia and into the closing ceremony, on independence day, as Zambia.

states.cue: Zanzibar has its own colour and a plain name; it is not the mainland's colour.

states.label: British protectorate

states.cue: Zanzibar carries "(Br.)" or Britain's colour: the sultan reigns, Britain rules.

states.cue: Zanzibar has its own colour and a plain name.

states.label: Part of Tanzania

states.cue: Zanzibar shares the mainland's colour; the country is Tanzania (or Tanganyika and Zanzibar).

transitions.funFact: In the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of 1890 Germany dropped its claims to Zanzibar in exchange for Heligoland, a speck of rock in the North Sea. That November Britain declared the sultanate its protectorate; six years later the shortest war in history, about forty minutes, confirmed who was in charge.

Zanzibar became independent again on 10 December 1963 as a constitutional sultanate. It lasted barely a month: a revolution on 12 January 1964 overthrew the sultan, and the island republic was soon talking union with Tanganyika.
Zanzibar united with Tanganyika on 26 April 1964, and in October the new country took a name blending both: Tanzania. Zanzibar still has its own president and parliament inside the union.

transitions.funFact: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took over the Ndebele and Shona lands from 1890 and, in May 1895, named its territory Rhodesia after its founder. In 1898 the part south of the Zambezi became Southern Rhodesia, one of very few countries named after a living person.

When Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia on 24 October 1964, Southern Rhodesia simply dropped the 'Southern'. A year later Ian Smith's white-minority government declared independence from Britain, which almost no country recognised; maps often printed 'Rhodesia (Br.)' or added a note.

After a long guerrilla war and a brief, unrecognised 'Zimbabwe Rhodesia' in 1979, the country became independent as Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980. The name comes from Great Zimbabwe, the stone city of a medieval Shona kingdom; dzimba dza mabwe means 'houses of stone'.
